"Most of the furniture that comes to the recycling center ends up in the incinerator." And that is a shame, because materials such as wood, metal, textile and foam can often be reused very well. That is why producers and importers of furniture will be made responsible by 2030 at the latest for the collection and recycling or reuse of the items they put on the market. Barbecue aprons and animal leashes More and more municipalities and public waste companies do not want to wait for that and have set up dismantling halls themselves. By now there are six of them across the Netherlands. Often people with a distance to the labor market take the furniture apart. One of the waste companies involved is Cure Afvalbeheer, which handles collection in <entity id="org:gemeente-eindhoven">Eindhoven</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-valkenswaard">Valkenswaard</entity> and <entity id="org:gemeente-geldrop-mierlo">Geldrop-Mierlo</entity>. "We take apart all box springs and sofas that we receive through the recycling centers," says Twan de Waal of Cure. "Sofas without staples and with a lot of cardboard are taken apart in 20 minutes. Others are harder and take half an hour." Box springs are even harder. "There is a hard wooden side nailed on. You almost can't get those staples out." Cure partly does this from the perspective of sustainability. The materials from the furniture are reused. For example, the plastic is used to make beer crates and shopping baskets, the wood is used for new bathroom furniture, and the leather is used for animal leashes and barbecue aprons. In addition, cost savings are an important motive. The more waste is incinerated, the more incineration tax has to be paid. And that hits furniture hard, precisely because it forms such a large and heavy waste mountain. "That tax is already very high and will become much higher in the coming years," says De Waal of Cure. Citizens feel that in their wallets through the waste charges they pay. That is why it pays to extract reusable materials. "The less we have to incinerate, the lower the waste charge." Better to repair Furniture manufacturers and importers will now pay the costs. "This creates an incentive for producers to make furniture that is easier to take apart, better to repair and reuse, and lasts longer," says NVRD director Eijer. A number of companies have already started themselves. For example, IKEA has a buy-back service and customers can repair their furniture with spare parts. Office furniture company Ahrend refurbishes office furniture to sell again. Mandatory reuse According to Eijer, it is mainly important that clear targets come with the introduction for more sustainable design and reuse of materials in furniture. For example, that a certain percentage must consist of recycled material. "Then a market will develop for it and it will become economically viable." Trade associations of furniture manufacturers CBM and RND support the introduction of producer responsibility. However, CBM says it must happen in a "workable way", and RND says data must first be available on how much furniture can be recycled and reused "in a profitable way" before targets are set. The municipalities hope for cooperation with the manufacturers. "Furniture producers take back as much old furniture as possible themselves when they sell new furniture. For the remaining part, municipalities are happy to help collect it," says NVRD director Eijer. The municipalities also expect to continue playing a role in recycling. "It will be quite difficult for companies to do that in a good way."

title: Arson at the railway, no trains between Rotterdam and Delft
lead: A fire was set at a railway bridge at Rotterdam-Delfshaven last night. This has major consequences for train traffic; it is at least at a standstill for the rest of the day between the Rotterdam Centraal and Delft Campus stations. Around 02:30 a fault occurred at the railway bridge. A contractor who went to investigate the fault saw that the door of a technical room had been ground open. Smouldering cables were inside. According to a spokesperson for rail infrastructure manager ProRail, a fire was set there. Sabotage is possible. The fire brigade has been present at the railway bridge over the Delfshavense Schie since last night. The fire has been put out and the technical room is being ventilated so that the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> can carry out its investigation. Once the police have finished the investigation, ProRail can only go inside to assess the damage and draw up a recovery plan. How large the damage is will therefore only become clear later. No trains It is certain that no trains will run between Rotterdam and Delft all day today. "I do not rule out that it could take longer", says a ProRail spokesperson. The track between Rotterdam and Delft is one of the busiest in the Netherlands and is also used by trains covering long distances, for example between the Randstad and Zeeland or Limburg. For travellers, this causes a lot of disruption. Travelling by train around the disruption is possible via Gouda; NS is deploying buses between Rotterdam Centraal and Delft station. <entity id="person:annet-bertram">Staatssecretaris Bertram</entity> of Infrastructure is shocked by the incident. "That this is arson and therefore deliberate I find very objectionable and worrying", she says.

title: Prominent figures leave NSC: 'Party has completely strayed'
lead: Former MPs Ilse Saris and Harm Holman have cancelled their membership of Nieuw Sociaal Contract, after Dirk Gotink, the last active NSC politician and a member of the European Parliament, left the party on Wednesday . The immediate reason is the invitation to Mona Keijzer to speak at the NSC party congress today. At the moment she took the floor, about half of the NSC members present left the hall. The party board confirms that this week even more members have expressed their dissatisfaction by cancelling their membership. In an internal message Saris writes: "In my eyes the party has completely strayed from what NSC stood for." Holman tells Nieuwsuur : "NSC was a reasonable centre party on content, but it has degenerated into an increasingly right-wing and populist party. And I don't feel at home in that." Holman has meanwhile rejoined the CDA. The party Nieuw Sociaal Contract was founded three years ago by former CDA member Pieter Omtzigt and won 20 seats in the House of Representatives that same year, out of nowhere. After taking part in a cabinet and Omtzigt's departure for health reasons, the party won 0 seats in the subsequent House of Representatives elections. Since then there has been a exodus of members, and one party figure after another is leaving. Quarrel Nicolien van Vroonhoven, former parliamentary group leader, has also cancelled her membership. She did so after the summer, due to a personal conflict with the party board. "I wrote a letter to the board and I wish them every success. The love between me and the party has cooled. I don't want to say much more about that." Former minister of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> Judith Uitermark has also not been a member of NSC for some time. "The movement I see in the party, I don't feel at home in that." Former state secretary Tjebbe van Oostenbruggen tells Nieuwsuur : "NSC is a closed book for me." Former MP Olger van Dijk is also among those cancelling, and wishes the party "all the best". Amateurish Former campaign leader and former MP Wytske Postma was there from the founding, but she no longer recognises the party of that time. According to her the party is caught up in an internal struggle and has become "a political amateur club". Postma sees the invitation to Mona Keijzer as a lurch to the right, which not everyone supports. The party was founded for good governance, and Keijzer has "a somewhat different style". According to Postma, an dissolution congress today would have been "sensible, however difficult that may be". During today's congress, half of those present left the hall when Keijzer took the floor. Party chairman Ronald de Bruin sees it differently. "We are in a difficult phase and we are a party without a leader. We have invited Mona Keijzer as a guest speaker to look for the common ground." According to a spokesperson for Keijzer, the talk will be about her new political movement Project 2029. Of the former MPs who are still members and whom Nieuwsuur has spoken to, most are not present at today's congress. In the event hall in Breda, about a hundred members were seated this Saturday. The party board ultimately did not survive a motion of no confidence and resigned.

title: Households will soon pay more for gas, increase in fixed energy contracts
lead: "The heating sometimes comes on already, but we keep in mind that it's expensive. So in the evening a blanket over you or a thick sweater on, that's what you're thinking about now." This customer, like other visitors to the DIY store, is occupied with autumn, which has now truly begun. Many households' heating is coming on again. The chance is high that turning the thermostat will cost more than last year. Because of the war in the Middle East, gas prices have been rising sharply for months. Tom Schuitemaker of comparison site Pricewise sees this too. "The price of gas compared to a year ago is really 40 to 50 cents higher per cubic metre. If you're around an average of 1000 cubic metres, then gas alone amounts to 500 euros per year. Add 250 for electricity, and it adds up quickly." How fast the gas price rose: At the end of October 2025 the average gas price for households was 1.19 euros per cubic metre. Yesterday that price was 1.60 euros. That is an increase of almost 35 percent. On the sites of price comparers an increase is visible in the number of people who want to fix their energy price, also see other providers such as Independer and Overstappen.nl. Notable is that for the first time contracts with a term of several years are slightly cheaper than annual contracts. That is partly because the expectation is that the supply of liquefied gas will increase in the coming years. There are three types of energy contracts. Variable, fixed and dynamic. With a fixed contract you lock in the same energy price for a longer period. For variable contracts there is no end date, but the energy supplier can adjust the price every few months. With a dynamic contract the price changes constantly, every day or even every hour. A fixed annual contract is normally advantageous because you get a discount from an energy company, for example in the form of a welcome bonus. But the 3-year contracts can now compete, says Schuitemaker. "We see that longer contracts are requested 10 times more often than a year ago." Gas price remains high for now: Autumn has only just begun and although temperatures are already dropping somewhat, it will get colder from November. Then demand for gas also increases. For households who want and can control their energy use, a dynamic energy contract is an option, says Gerben Hieminga, senior sector economist energy markets and energy policy at ING. For example, charging your electric car during the day when the sun shines or doing the laundry. For people who want to avoid risks, a fixed contract is an alternative. "If it becomes a cold winter, prices will shoot up. If you want to avoid that risk, you should take a fixed contract." Economist Hieminga expects prices to remain high for now. Schuitemaker of Pricewise thinks so too. Because of the unrest in the Middle East there is less supply for now, and it does not look like that situation will change within a short time.

title: Nuisance caused by a group of youths in Heerenveen: 'They tie gas cylinders to fireworks'
lead: The municipality of Heerenveen has been dealing with a large group of nuisance-causing youths for weeks. Among other things, they set off fireworks in the evenings. "It is no longer just ordinary fireworks. They tie bottles of turpentine and gas cylinders to them", says council member Nando Vries at Omrop <entity id="org:provincie-fryslan">Fryslân</entity> . The council member of Heerenveen Lokaal, the largest faction in the municipal council, says the impact on some residents and entrepreneurs is great. "We had a resident on the line crying because they no longer dare to go out in the evening." Mayor <entity id="person:avine-fokkens-kelder">Avine Fokkens-Kelder</entity> says that a lot is being done behind the scenes to tackle the nuisance. "The municipality and <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> have been in consultation with each other for weeks and a flex team of the police has been deployed." A flex team consists of extra officers who are deployed in a problem-oriented way. " Since Friday we also have concrete names in view." Cat-and-mouse game It has not been announced how many youths are involved. According to Fokkens-Kelder, it was a challenge to map out the nuisance-causers because of the "cat-and-mouse game" between the agencies and the youths. The youths are, among other things, being called to a conversation with the mayor. "But other measures can also be taken, ranging from fines to an area ban", according to the mayor. The mayor also appeals to parents. "I hope people at home have the conversation about what young people get up to in the evenings." The Drenthe town of <entity id="org:gemeente-hoogeveen">Hoogeveen</entity> has also been plagued by nuisance from youths for days. There too, the municipality is intervening. For example, the police can carry out preventive searches in the evenings, cameras are hanging in the centre and a ban on gathering applies.

title: New proposal for billions less EU budget still not sufficient for cabinet
lead: Ireland, as the half-yearly EU presidency, has made a proposal to cut the EU budget for the coming years. Ireland proposes removing 140 billion from it. The upcoming seven-year budget is the subject of much discussion. The Netherlands and five other countries think the European Commission wants too large a budget. The European Commission had proposed a multiannual budget of 1.76 trillion euros (1760 billion). In a letter to EU presidency Ireland, the prime ministers of the Netherlands, Germany, Sweden, Denmark, Austria and Finland urged that the budget be cut by hundreds of billions of euros. The countries, which like to call themselves the frugal six, think that less money should go to farmers and poorer regions in the EU. Traditionally those regions receive about two thirds of the budget. The countries instead advocate more investment in security, defence, economic competitiveness, innovation and the fight against illegal migration. In the Irish proposal, 3 percent is removed from the budget proposed by the Commission for, among other things, agriculture, fisheries and poorer regions. Under the heading security, competitiveness and prosperity, the Irish plan instead removes 13 percent of the budget proposed by the Commission. That therefore goes against the wish of the Netherlands, among others, to spend more money on exactly that. Inflation The current budget, which runs until and including 2027, is 1.2 trillion euros. With the Irish proposal, the EU budget still rises by billions to 1.62 trillion. That is an increase of 30 percent, but 8 percent less than the European Commission's proposal. That increase of 30 percent does not mean the European Commission can do much more with it, because inflation makes money worth less. The European Covid debts of 750 billion euros must also be fully repaid by 2050 at the latest. Due to higher interest rates, repayment has become more expensive. The new Irish proposal is part of negotiations that have been ongoing for months and will be discussed next week. On Thursday and Friday the European leaders meet for an EU summit. Netherlands opposes new proposal. The cabinet has already indicated that the new proposal is also insufficient. <entity id="person:eelco-heinen">Minister Heinen</entity> of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-financien">Financiën</entity> says in a written response: "The Netherlands cannot agree to this proposal either. The Netherlands wants to see a much larger reduction of the budget together with other countries. We are therefore sending the proposal back immediately." The German government is also not yet satisfied. Chancellor Merz says that "we are still far from" an agreement. Many other EU countries, including Spain and Italy, on the other hand want to hold on to support for agriculture and poorer regions and for more money to go there. In the end, all 27 member states must agree to the budget.

title: Wrong-way driver killed in accident on the A2, road closed for hours
lead: In an accident on the A2 near Breukelen, a wrong-way driver died early in the afternoon, the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> reports. The identity of the wrong-way driver has not yet been released. According to witnesses, the driver initially drove on the motorway towards Utrecht. At one point the motorist ended up on the other carriageway. At the Breukelen exit he collided with two other cars. Debris was scattered across at least four lanes: The driver of one of those cars was injured. The driver of the other vehicle was unharmed. Motorway closed The motorway towards Amsterdam is closed for investigation. This is expected to last until 18.00 hours. The police are conducting an investigation and are looking for witnesses and dashcam footage. Because of the accident there is a traffic jam of an hour and a half, writes RTV Utrecht. Traffic is being diverted from junction Oudenrijn via the A12, A27 and A1.

title: Train traffic around Schiphol disrupted for hours by power outage
lead: A power outage this afternoon caused problems for train traffic to and from Schiphol. As a result, it was busy at the airport. Also, fewer trains ran between Amsterdam-Zuid, Schiphol and Hoofddorp. Around 15.30 the outage was resolved. The timetable was then restarted. It will still take a while before train traffic runs again according to the normal timetable, says a spokesperson for NS. Also switch fault According to the railway manager ProRail, a power outage occurred in a high-voltage cabinet at Amsterdam Riekerpolder, just before the branch to Amsterdam Lelylaan and Amsterdam-Zuid. "We replaced a defective component, which resolved the outage," said ProRail. The cause of the defect is still being investigated. There were more problems on the rail network today. For example, fewer trains are running between The Hague, Leiden and Rotterdam and between Rotterdam and Dordrecht due to a switch fault. Also, no trains are running between Rotterdam and Delft due to arson this morning at a rail bridge in Delfshaven. It may be sabotage.

title: Jan G. stayed hidden in Overasselt for another twelve hours after escape, this is how he managed to get away
lead: After dozens of armed men had appeared at his gate and shot his bodyguard dead, Jan G. was still in Overasselt for a large part of the day. The convicted drug criminal had fled to family elsewhere in the village. Omroep <entity id="org:provincie-gelderland">Gelderland</entity> spoke with several sources in Overasselt and, in collaboration with the NOS, reconstructed Jan G.'s flight after the outbreak of violence on 1 September at his house. Not yet suspecting what awaited him that night, the 28-year-old Jan G. stepped into the local supermarket in Overasselt on Monday evening, 31 August. It would be the last time for now that he visited the supermarket. A few hours later, around four in the morning, G. was woken in his chalet on Ewijkseweg by the alarm of his security system. The camera footage showed a group of more than thirty men armed to the teeth. Three of them had earlier that evening tried to break into a house on Honingklaver in Overasselt. A brother-in-law of Jan G. lives here. Alerted by the camera footage, G. fled with his girlfriend and their two young children through a rear exit of the grounds. His parents were still sleeping in a barn elsewhere on the 600 square metre plot. G. and his girlfriend probably walked along a path through a dried-up ditch to hide in the bushes at the edge of a meadow. G. had ordered bodyguard Berry 'urgently'. Meanwhile the armed men had arrived at his home on Ewijkseweg. One of them shot bodyguard Berry, who was sitting in his car at that moment. Shortly before, eye to eye with the group, Berry had called his employer in panic. His employer texted him that he must leave. But by then it was already too late. The bodyguard died of his wounds. Jan G. had ordered bodyguard Berry 'urgently' from a security service two days earlier, after two suspicious persons had walked past his house. Shortly after Berry's death, two police officers who rushed in were also shot. They were seriously wounded. As emergency services flocked in en masse, the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> launched a manhunt for the more than thirty suspects. G. and his family were meanwhile picked up by an acquaintance, who took them to his house elsewhere in Overasselt, less than 1200 metres from Ewijkseweg 6. The police rang the doorbell at G.'s house and found his mother there. Once inside the barn, where she and her husband live, the officers saw G.'s father, also a convicted drug criminal. He said: "Get lost, you idiots. Who are you to tell me what to do? I'm not going anywhere at all." The man and the woman were told to stay in the barn and keep the doors closed. Around five in the morning G. contacted the boss of the shot bodyguard and told him that Berry had died. Hiding in Overasselt. While the chaos around Ewijkseweg continued, G. remained in hiding with his family in Overasselt. According to neighbours, the fleeing suspects were unaware that they were running near the house where their target was hiding. Only at the end of the afternoon did a taxi arrive here, after which G. got in with his family and left. The municipality closed the house on Ewijkseweg for a year and imposed an area ban on G. During the day a video surfaced in which criminals demanded compensation from him for a lost consignment of 1283 kilos of cocaine. Visit to collect passports. From that moment on, G. with his family, his parents, and two brothers-in-law with their families had disappeared from the village. Where they are is unclear. In the weeks after the attack, the municipality, under police escort, entered the sealed-off grounds on Ewijkseweg twice more. According to someone in the know, G.'s girlfriend was allowed to briefly return during one of those visits to collect essential items, such as identity documents. The house reportedly had been completely turned upside down during several police investigations. The animals that stayed on the grounds, including horses and large guard dogs, have been placed in boarding facilities. Arrest in Germany. On 18 September G. was arrested in Germany at the request of the Dutch authorities. He is suspected of involvement in the import of cocaine via the port of Dunkirk. According to German police, he was travelling towards the Netherlands via the A44 motorway from the direction of Saxony-Anhalt. Since then G. has been held in a German cell. He still speaks with his lawyer from time to time, but meanwhile a court case looms in Den Bosch. There he will have to answer for his involvement in the cocaine case surrounding Dunkirk, on top of all the other problems that are dogging him. Interviews with those involved. This story is based on a large number of conversations that the authors conducted over the past five weeks with people directly involved in the Overasselt case. All conversations were held on the basis of anonymity. Information from other sources and from official bodies was also used.

title: 18.000 chickens dead in large fire in Zeeuws-Vlaanderen
lead: A very large fire raged this afternoon in a chicken barn in Biervliet in Zeeuws-Vlaanderen. The 18.000 chickens did not survive the fire, a spokesperson for the safety region confirmed to Omroep Zeeland. The fire released a lot of thick, black smoke that could be seen from far away. The Veiligheidsregio Zeeland (VRZ) warned residents to keep windows and doors closed. Cause unknown According to the regional broadcaster, it concerns an organic laying hen barn. The fire broke out around 15.00 hours. The cause is still unknown. There were no people present in the barn. Three fire engines were deployed to fight the fire. A crane is also being deployed to break open the barn. Around 16.30 hours the fire was reported under control. The fire brigade will still be busy for some time extinguishing remaining hot spots.

title: Injured in attack on airport in Saudi capital Riyad, air traffic at a standstill
lead: An unknown number of people have been injured in attacks on the international airport in the Saudi capital Riyad. Two regional officials say the airport has been evacuated after a missile hit a passenger terminal. According to witnesses, ambulances were rushing to the airport. All air traffic to and from King Khalid International Airport has been halted. A source at a local hospital told news agency AFP that dozens of people were injured in the attack. He saw gate 401 of the domestic terminal being hit. "I saw the injured with my own eyes. Everyone ran away." Data from Flightaware shows that at least 225 flights at King Khalid International Airport have been cancelled in the past 24 hours, following the earlier attacks on the airport this week. The airport calls on travelers to contact their airline and check the status of their flight before coming to the airport. Several airlines have already taken measures. Kuwait Airways cancelled all flights to and from Riyad today. Several embassies in Riyhad, including the US embassy, have called on their citizens to avoid the international airport and the surrounding area. Yemen The attack comes two days after the Iran-backed Houthi rebels attacked the airport in Riyad. Three Saudis lost their lives in that attack, including a pilot. That international airports are targeted in a series of attacks is exceptional. Earlier this week the Houthis also attacked airfields in the Saudi towns of Jizan, Najran and Abha. These lie a few tens of kilometers from the border with Yemen. Saudi Arabia supports the Yemeni government army, which is fighting the Houthi rebels. Since the start of the large-scale Operation Dawn of Yemen by the Yemeni army last Monday, the Houthis have stepped up their attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia. The European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) has tightened its guidelines for Saudi airspace. It points to the Houthis' ability to hit targets deeper in the kingdom, including Riyad, and to their "greater focus on aviation infrastructure". The missile and drone attacks, as well as the attempts to intercept them, "increase the risk that civil aircraft will be hit", the agency says. Under fire Meanwhile, the fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces continues. Saudi Arabia is providing air support to the internationally recognized government in Yemen in an attempt to reverse the Houthis' recent territorial gains along the Red Sea. Because of the situation in Yemen, some 200,000 people have fled, including to Djibouti, a small country in the Horn of Africa. The UN migration and refugee agency (IOM) called on countries this week to take action. Saudi Arabia has sought support from the US and other allies, now that its airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure are under fire. This concerns, among other things, sharing intelligence and planning and identifying targets. 'I am not happy' When the American president Trump left the White House yesterday, he was asked about the attacks on the airport in Riyad. "It is not good" and "I am not happy", he told reporters. For now there are no signs of American military support in response to the attacks. The ministers of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> of Saudi Arabia and Oman spoke by phone this week about the importance of "support for diplomatic solutions to reduce tensions in the region". Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, regularly acts as a mediator. But there is not yet any prospect of a solution to the escalation.

title: Municipalities want more money for resilience against disasters and threats
lead: Municipalities feel they are receiving too little money from the national government to make themselves resilient against all kinds of threats. These include, for example, cyber and hybrid threats or dangers arising from climate change, such as nature fires. <entity id="person:sharon-dijksma">Sharon Dijksma</entity>, chair of the Association of Netherlands Municipalities (<entity id="org:vereniging-van-nederlandse-gemeenten">VNG</entity>), says that for the resilience task municipalities need several times what is budgeted in the Miljoenennota. "I assume that in total it really is a matter of hundreds of millions." "<entity id="org:kabinet">Het kabinet</entity> has earmarked 35 million for emergency support points and now, in the Miljoenennota, has added a gradually increasing series of 20 to 70 million for digital resilience, socio-societal resilience and continuity alike. But the gap between what municipalities need and what the cabinet is making available is therefore large," says the VNG. <entity id="org:gemeente-rotterdam">Rotterdam</entity> also wants more money. The Rotterdam port is often cited as a possible target for threats from Russia. "Resilience goes further than emergency support points, after all. We must also invest in society itself, in a strong social fabric that helps us during an emergency and in the recovery afterwards," says a spokesperson for the municipality. No evacuation facilities. The VNG already has a fairly clear picture of how municipalities would like to deploy extra money. "You can think of neighbourhood emergency plans and training for residents. We still need to talk with the ministry of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-justitie-en-veiligheid">Justitie en Veiligheid</entity> about sheltering and evacuation, for which there are now almost no facilities." "Emergency generators, satellite phones and pagers are needed, and the emergency services need many more resources, such as fire engines. The list is too long to list everything." VNG chair Dijksma, who is also <entity id="pos:burgemeester-utrecht">burgemeester van Utrecht</entity>, does have an idea of what needs to happen in her municipality. "We have many vulnerable residents who are not self-reliant, and they do not always have the money to prepare. We also need money for communication tools that we still lack." In Austerlitz, a village in the <entity id="org:gemeente-zeist">gemeente Zeist</entity>, people do not want to wait until municipalities have sufficient resources for safety exercises. Austerlitz lies in the middle of the forest and has few access roads. Because residents feared they would not be able to get away properly in the event of a major forest fire, volunteers set up a 'forest fire working group'. Today the volunteers of the working group practised as if a major forest fire was raging: "I am part of the group of citizens who keep an eye on everything when there is a risk of nature fires," says Robert Schliessler. "We work together with the safety region and train for what happens when our village is threatened." Today Schliessler is also taking part in the first exercise together with the safety region. "We have a WhatsApp group in the village, with six hundred people in it, and they will all be told there when the exercise begins. We have been asking the safety region for this exercise for three years and are super happy that it is finally here," he adds. "By now we work well together with the municipality and the safety region." The idea is that the group of volunteers keeps a close eye on 112 reports and passes on to residents that evacuation is needed. "We do that earlier than the emergency services. We have three locations where people can find each other, and these are determined at the moment we know where the fire is." 'Cannot be financed'. Dijksma is very positive about the exercise in Austerlitz. "It is very important that people also prepare themselves; these kinds of initiatives are gold." Municipal resilience falls under the Ministry of Justice and Security, and <entity id="person:david-van-weel">Minister Van Weel</entity> is also pleased with the initiative. "I am glad that challenges are being identified and that these kinds of things are being picked up and improved locally." Van Weel can certainly follow the call of the municipalities for more money. "In the Miljoenennota we have designated resilience as an important theme, but our spending will not cover all wishes," he says. "It is an enormous task, so I am not going to say we can do everything at once. We cannot finance that." According to the minister, municipalities can certainly get to work with the money they already receive, for example to work on the resilience of their critical processes. "Ultimately, resilience lies in the communities where people live; municipalities have a very large role in that."

title: Until at least 23.00 no trains between Rotterdam and Delft after arson
lead: No trains will run between Rotterdam and Delft until at least 23.00. The reason is the arson last night at a railway bridge in Rotterdam-Delfshaven. ProRail does not rule out that sabotage is involved. According to the railway manager, it will take until at least Sunday evening before the damage is repaired. Trains may not run on the route again until Monday morning. The railway between Rotterdam and Delft is one of the busiest routes in the Netherlands. It is also used by trains covering long distances, for example between the Randstad and Zeeland or Limburg. For train travellers, this also means a lot of inconvenience tomorrow. Eight-hour check According to ProRail, it is certain that the fire was deliberately started last night. The fire started last night in the technical room. The door to it had been pried open and inside lay smouldering cables. Research shows that 35 cables were damaged. Fifteen of them have burned through completely and must be replaced and re-welded. After replacing all cables, various checks must be carried out to determine whether the trains can run safely again. These checks take about eight hours. Whether sabotage was actually committed on the railway again must still be investigated by the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> and fire brigade. No one has been arrested yet.

title: From our correspondent... Boris van der Spek (Central America)
lead: Van onze Correspondent is a series by the makers of the podcast De Dag. Every Sunday we get to know one of the NOS correspondents, the country where they live and the stories that, in their view, deserve more attention. Today: Boris van der Spek, correspondent in Central America. Listen here: You can listen to this episode of De Dag via <entity id="org:zbo-nederlandse-publieke-omroep">NPO</entity> Luister and all other podcast apps. Do you like it? Then don't forget to subscribe. After studying journalism, Boris moved to Latin America. After a trip in his youth, he wanted to go back there. And he had long dreamed of becoming a correspondent on that continent. Methodically, he ticked off the ingredients needed to become a correspondent: speaking the language, having been there once, and falling in love. After meeting his current wife, Boris moved to Chile. There he worked as a correspondent for the first time and set up his own news outlet. Eventually the Chilean <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> visited his in-laws after he had written a story. "That made me very angry." After eight years he had had enough of Chile: "You want to do more, but newspapers were not waiting for a story from the country every week". Chaos. And then there was Mexico. "A wonderful chaos," Boris said. You have to be careful, with the drug cartels calling the shots in some places. "Fields are full of mines, there are ever heavier weapons on the streets. And that's just Mexico, you know, you're not in a war zone." But the Mexicans Boris meets are warm, invite him to stay for dinner and to sleep over, and teach him a lot about life. "I find how Mexicans deal with death very inspiring. Through rituals and ceremonies, my late mother stays alive." Going back to the Netherlands is not an option for now: "That would be too great a culture shock". Boris would rather stay for years more on the continent of his dreams: Latin America. Next week in our series: Van onze correspondent Mustafa Marghadi, the correspondent in Southeast Asia. Do you have a question for him? Email dedag@nos.nl Presentation & editing: Marco Geijtenbeek Editorial: Wouter Sloekers

title: Northern lights visible in parts of the Netherlands (but only through a camera)
lead: Between the rain showers, the northern lights could be seen last night and overnight. At least, through a lens. The so-called photographic northern lights cannot be seen with the naked eye, but a camera can capture them. Especially in the southern half of the country, people had a chance to capture the northern lights. There was less cloud cover there than in the north. Via NOS Ooggetuige, photos of the natural phenomenon came in from Limburg, South Holland and Gelderland. The colourful glow is caused by a solar storm: an eruption of electrically charged particles from the sun. Energy is released in the process, resulting in the play of colours in the sky. Northern lights, also known as aurora borealis, were regularly visible in the Netherlands in recent years because there was maximum solar activity then. That will be less in the coming years, so the chance of seeing it is smaller. "In the quiet period, around 2030, the chance of seeing the northern lights in the Netherlands is very small", says the <entity id="org:koninklijk-nederlands-meteorologisch-instituut">KNMI</entity> .

title: Leaders of Indian Cockroach Movement released after one day
lead: Founder Abhijeet Dipke and two other leaders of the Indian Cockroach Movement are free again. Dipke's lawyer confirms reports to that effect in Indian media. According to the movement's legal adviser, the condition set is that the three do not take part in disturbances of public order for one year. The trio was arrested yesterday after they arrived in Delhi by plane. The Cockroach Movement had called on its supporters to take to the streets en masse on Saturday and today to demand the departure of chairman Kumar of the national election commission. The arrest of the three leaders yesterday: The police were out in force yesterday to prevent demonstrators from going to the centre of Delhi. According to news agency Reuters, more than 2000 people were arrested there and another 400 in the city of Mumbai. According to the police, most were released last night. Besides members and supporters of the Cockroach Movement, journalists and opposition parliamentarians were also arrested, including a number of former ministers. The Cockroach Movement demands Kumar's departure because his election commission removed 130 million names from lists of Indians eligible to vote. That would benefit Prime Minister Modi, because it is mainly Muslims who would not vote for his Hindu-nationalist BJP party. According to the election commission, it concerns a clean-up operation. For example, 63 million names are said to have been removed of people who have moved, and 28 million are said to be names of deceased persons. 30 million people could not be traced, the election commission said.

title: Widespread outrage over attack on Riyadh airport: 'Dangerous escalation'
lead: The attack by Houthi rebels on the airport of the Saudi capital Riyadh is being widely condemned internationally. World leaders speak of a deliberate attack on a civilian target and call it a dangerous escalation of the fighting on the Arabian Peninsula. Twelve people died and more than 300 were injured when the passenger terminal was hit yesterday afternoon. It is thus the most serious attack on a Saudi target since fighting in Yemen flared up again halfway through this year. Earlier this week the airport was also hit by an attack from Yemen. Only limited footage of the attack is available because Saudi Arabia has strict censorship. Anyone who shares footage of attacks or damage may face a severe penalty. Several embassies have therefore advised their nationals not to post or forward footage. Nevertheless, some footage of the attack came out: UN envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg calls the attack a serious escalation. "These kinds of actions pose a serious threat to regional security, perpetuate a cycle of violence and hamper the search for peace in Yemen." UN chief Guterres calls the attack on a civilian target a violation of international law. "This must stop immediately." Canadian Prime Minister Carney also says that "there is no justification whatsoever for attacks on civilian infrastructure". For the Netherlands, <entity id="person:tom-berendsen">minister Berendsen</entity> of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> condemns the attack. "The Netherlands stands in full solidarity with the people of Saudi Arabia and our Gulf partners." Retaliation A Houthi spokesperson has claimed responsibility for the attack in a statement to The New York Times. According to him, it is direct retaliation for Saudi attacks on his country in which civilians died. According to his count, 91 people have died since 3 September, mainly women and children. "The world must understand that airports, ports, weddings, funerals, hospitals and markets in Yemen are civilian targets that you should not attack," he reasons. "That applies both to Yemen and elsewhere." American interference? The American president Trump, in a conversation with journalists, did not want to say whether American armed forces would support Saudi Arabia's fight against the Houthis. The US carried out several attacks on the Houthis shortly after Trump took office last year, but recently turned down Saudi requests for support. "Who knows, we will look into it," Trump answered evasively when asked whether he was reconsidering his position. "We have only just heard of the recent attack, so we will still have to decide. We will do so quickly." He called the attack on the airport "terrible". Analysts pointed out earlier that the US is now focused mainly on the conflict with Iran and therefore is not waiting for a second front in the region. Moreover, the American weapons arsenal is said to already be depleted by the attacks on Iran and the defence against counterattacks from that country. Tirade over Nobel Prize: After his short answer about the crisis in the Middle East, Trump took longer to lash out at the Norwegian Nobel Committee over its choice of jurist Navi Pallay. He once again repeated his incorrect claim that he had ended eight wars, freed hostages in Israel and prevented a conflict between China and Taiwan. "I've stopped eight wars and then they give the Nobel Prize to someone nobody has ever heard of. I had never heard of her, nobody I know had ever heard of her," Trump said. "Something is wrong in Norway, I can tell you that." Trump has in the past made no secret that he himself would like to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Recently he said that "the US, with me as its representative, should have received the Nobel Prize". That this did not happen he called an "indelible stain" on Norway's reputation.

title: Americans fire on cargo ship that reportedly left Iran earlier
lead: A cargo ship became disabled in the Gulf of Oman after an American attack. According to the Americans, the ship had left Iran beforehand and did not comply with the American blockade imposed on ships from Iran. "An American fighter aircraft struck the rear of the Panama-flagged ship Ocean Molica with a precision weapon. As a result, the ship could no longer proceed under its own power. The crew remained unharmed," the American Central Command said. Central Command is responsible for the American military in the Middle East, Central Asia and parts of South Asia. The Americans' statement is practically impossible to verify. News agency Reuters tried to contact the owner of the ship but did not succeed. It is unclear what has happened to the crew. What is certain is that the ship had switched off its AIS beacon, with which it can always be tracked and which should in principle always be on. The last known position is off the coast of Oman on 5 October. Ships switch off this beacon more often in the dangerous part of the waterway. Since 14 July the Americans have been trying to stop ships leaving Iran. Since then, according to Central Command, four cargo ships have been "disabled". Another 135 ships reportedly turned back after warnings and returned to Iranian waters. In the same period, the Americans say they destroyed ten oil tankers linked to the Iranian Revolutionary Guard. Control: Iran and America both try to claim control over the Strait of Hormuz by imposing conditions on ships. As far as Iran is concerned, ships may only pass through the strait via a route set by Iran and only with permission from the strictly Islamic country. That permission follows payment of a percentage of the total value of the cargo the ship is carrying. Shipowners who do not comply risk an attack on their ship. America is stopping all ships leaving Iranian waters. Anyone who does not respect the blockade runs the risk of being attacked, as the Panamanian ship was this weekend. According to the International Maritime Organization (IMO), at least 93 ships have been hit by violence since the start of the conflict on 28 February. 24 people died as a result. Evasion: The claims of both countries to the strait are not watertight, several media outlets noted earlier. By switching off all communication systems, such as AIS, ships still manage to evade the blockades. Those who succeed are well paid. Captains and their crews receive bonuses of thousands of euros per day if they venture into the Strait of Hormuz, the Financial Times wrote this week. The Strait of Hormuz is generally considered vital to the world economy. Before the conflict between America and Iran broke out, about 20 percent of all oil and liquefied natural gas was transported through the strait. Because of the Iranian and American blockades, energy prices worldwide have risen to record levels.

title: 14 dead in two family murders in Pennsylvania and Georgia
lead: Two family murders in the US over this weekend have left fourteen people dead in total. A shooting in Pennsylvania killed nine people, and a separate incident in Georgia killed five more. In both cases the perpetrator was also among the dead. In Pennsylvania the massacre took place in the city of Erie, about 200 kilometers from Pittsburgh. Here a 45-year-old man shot several family members and a friend of one of them. The police have not yet announced the motive or the exact relationship to the victims. Officers went to investigate around 17.00 local time after a report of shots. In front of a house, two shot women aged 51 and 37 were found. Robot reconnaissance. The police then searched the building with a robot and a drone and found more victims. Among the victims were a woman who was 8 months pregnant, a 5-year-old boy and a one-year-old girl. Other victims were between 19 and 44. "Out of respect for the victims we will not describe what we found inside," a police chief announced at a press conference. It is clear that the shooter took his own life: he was found dead on the first floor of the building. Dispute over smoking. In the small town of Douglas in Georgia, the family violence was discovered around 23.00 after an emergency call from one of the victims. This woman had managed to flee the house severely injured, but died on the way to hospital. Here too it appears to be a series of murders followed by a suicide. According to the police, all four victims were family of the perpetrator. Nothing has yet been made public about their identities, except that they were five adults. Here too it is unclear what the motive was. However, it turns out that the police had been called earlier that day by the perpetrator's wife. She complained that her husband was smoking indoors and so "murdered her with the smoke". Need help? Are you thinking about suicide or worried about someone? Talking about suicide helps and can be done anonymously via the chat at www.113.nl or by phone on 113 or 0800-0113.

title: Rainbow flag flown across the country, flags stolen in Oldebroek
lead: The much-discussed rainbow flag flies at <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>. The flag was raised in connection with Coming Out Day, a day on which there is extra attention worldwide for coming out. It is the first time the rainbow flag hangs at the representative body. Flags have also been hung throughout the country, but in the Gelderland municipality of Oldebroek several rainbow flags have been stolen. The municipality decided this week to scrap its LGBTI policy, and therefore also not to hoist a flag. That decision led to much discussion in the municipality. In protest, residents of Oldebroek hung up flags. At the Kruiskerk in the municipality, a rainbow flag was raised yesterday in the presence of dozens of people. 'Colourfulness' According to Reverend Han Wilmink, the flag is in fact a Christian symbol. "It shows the colourfulness of God's creation and everyone belongs to that. We will not leave anyone aside here." The residents' action soon met resistance: on Saturday evening it became clear that several flags had been stolen, including the flag at the church. De Stentor reports that some flagpoles were even vandalised. Meanwhile a new flag hangs at the church. How the issue is playing out in Oldebroek (and divides the municipality) you can read here: In <entity id="org:gemeente-alblasserdam">Alblasserdam</entity> tempers also ran high. There the flag was already flying two days ago. The hoisting was not announced in advance. The municipality then published a post on social media with the text: "In Alblasserdam there is room for everyone". Swastikas were placed under the post, the local paper writes. In addition, people called for the flag or the flagpole to be removed by force. The comments under the post have since been disabled. Vote on the flag. In the Tweede Kamer the hoisting of the flag led to much discussion. The presidium, the daily board of the Tweede Kamer, first decided to hoist the rainbow flag. But after opposition from the Christian opposition party the SGP, that plan did not go ahead. Other opposition parties then however submitted a motion to nevertheless have the flag hoisted on Coming Out Day. On Thursday evening a vote by roll call was held, after which it became clear that a majority of the House wanted to have the flag flying next to the parliament building after all.

title: New search for aviation pioneer Earhart on atoll in South Pacific
lead: "If you find this, you have a find comparable to finding the Titanic," says aviation expert Joris Melkert (TU Delft). "Then you have really scored." Melkert is referring to the wreck of the aircraft of the world-famous American aviation pioneer Amelia Earhart. She disappeared without a trace in 1937 during a flight around the world, together with her navigator Fred Noonan. "One of the great mysteries in the history of aviation," says Melkert. Tomorrow an expedition of American scientists arrives on the remote coral island Nikumaroro in the South Pacific. Earhart, Noonan and their aircraft have been searched for there more often. In vain. Six years ago the search for what happened to them got a new boost, because the wreck would be visible on a satellite photo. Earhart and Noonan departed on 1 June 1937 with their aircraft Electra from Miami for a flight around the world. They flew eastward, roughly along the line of the equator. The journey went smoothly. On 29 June they had already covered 37,000 kilometres. On 2 July they took off in Papua New Guinea for the last part of the trip: the crossing of the Pacific Ocean. The first stopover was to be Howland Island, a flight of 20 hours. A ship of the American coast guard was waiting there to guide the Electra with radio signals to Howland Island. But something went wrong. For some reason Earhart and Noonan failed to make good contact and to receive the directional instructions. They could not find Howland Island and flew on. Out of fuel. "I think at some point the fuel ran out and that they ended up in the sea," says Melkert. That was also the conclusion of the investigation by the American government shortly after the disappearance, and of later researchers. The Electra would, after the crash, not far from Howland Island, have sunk kilometres deep to the bottom of the ocean. There are also other theories. Possibly the two searched for another landing place and so ended up at the uninhabited atoll Nikumaroro. Earlier investigations on site yielded nothing concrete, but the satellite photo from 2020 fed the theory that the flight of Earhart and Noonan had ended there. Researchers from the American Purdue University found that object on the satellite photo also on an aerial photo of Nikumaroro from 1938. Also bones. Melkert remains sceptical. "That is 650 km south of the island where she should actually have arrived, so that already makes it less likely that it succeeded," he says. "But anyway, some bones were found there earlier of someone who could possibly be a woman." "And then somewhere just off the coast of that atoll there is something that could be an aircraft. So the idea is: this could perhaps be it, so let's go and take a look."

title: Governments cherish oil refineries due to high fuel prices
lead: High prices at the pump and an impending diesel shortage are leading to a different view of the future of the oil refineries in Rotterdam and Vlissingen. Although the oil era is coming to an end due to climate policy, petrol, diesel and kerosene are still needed for now. Governments want to prevent production capacity from declining faster than demand for oil products. Europe currently depends partly on imports from abroad for diesel and kerosene. Because of the war in the Middle East, businesses and consumers are paying record prices for these. The European Commission wants to get rid of this dependence. President Von der Leyen therefore announced this week a "strategic dialogue" on refineries in Europe: "The goal is to lower costs and to have enough stocks, also for defence." Earlier, NATO Secretary General Rutte already warned of a shortage of diesel for tanks and kerosene for combat aircraft in a possible war situation. Next week, climate minister Stientje van Veldhoven will present the plans for the future of refining in the Netherlands. Key position in Europe. The Netherlands plays a very large role in the production of petrol, diesel and kerosene. The refineries of Shell, BP and ExxonMobil in Rotterdam and the Zeeland Refinery in Vlissingen produce tens of billions of litres of fuel for the European market. This summer they made somewhat more kerosene because of shortages in aviation; at the moment somewhat more diesel is being made again. The costs of producing fuels are higher in Europe than in other parts of the world. This is partly due to the price of CO2 rights that companies must buy in order to be allowed to emit greenhouse gases. In addition, electricity costs in the Netherlands are higher than in neighbouring countries and it is difficult to get a heavy grid connection. The challenge for <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> is now to ensure that refineries that will ultimately have to disappear keep producing optimally in the short term. At the same time, CO2 emissions must be reduced further. In addition, faster progress must be made on developing sustainable alternatives to diesel and kerosene. This concerns, among other things, green hydrogen and biofuels. The largest refinery in Europe is Shell's in Pernis. Every day just over 400,000 barrels of crude oil are converted into fuels here. A year ago Shell cancelled the construction of a bio-refinery for sustainable diesel and kerosene, even though more than half a billion euros had already been invested in it. The reason was competition from Asia and an insufficient blending obligation for biodiesel and bio-kerosene, according to the company. Five years ago Shell already produced the first synthetic kerosene in its laboratory for a KLM flight to Madrid. This sustainable aviation fuel is made from green hydrogen and CO2. According to Shell, the market for synthetic fuels is not yet ready for mass production. That does not mean nothing is happening in Rotterdam. Shell has built the first large factory for green hydrogen in the Netherlands. The Finnish Neste produces biofuels on the Tweede Maasvlakte and is currently doubling production to 2.7 million tonnes per year. The Dutch company Power2X is working on a factory for synthetic kerosene. The location lies exactly between the refineries of Shell and Exxon Mobil. Profits in the billions. To emit less CO2, Shell and Exxon Mobil are taking part in capturing and storing CO2. The greenhouse gases from the refineries are then partly stored in an empty gas field under the North Sea. In the coming years, capturing and storing CO2 will further increase the costs of refining. Building new oil refineries is not an obvious choice given the approaching end of the oil era. Shell has already more than halved the number of refineries worldwide in recent years. The Gunvor refinery in Rotterdam was closed last year. To maintain sufficient refining capacity in Europe, costs must not deviate too much from those on other continents. Because so much fuel is made in Rotterdam and Zeeland, other European countries are also looking at the Netherlands. Limiting costs for refineries is not uncontroversial. The oil giants are currently making billions in profits every quarter because of high fuel prices. The environmental movement will not thank the minister of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-kgg">Klimaat en Groene Groei</entity> if support comes for the production of diesel and kerosene.

title: Fans may take a piece of the New York metro home
lead: Harlem, Uptown, 42nd Street, or simply do not cross the tracks. Signs with these inscriptions and other discarded pieces could be bought by metro fans last week at the annual flea market of the New York metro. Transport operator MTA started five years ago with a two-day sale of outdated materials: station signs, trash cans, and the grab holds commuters can hold onto when there is no seat. The seats themselves are also being sold, by the way: a three-seater for 1000 dollars, and with one seat fewer you pay 650 dollars. For the iconic signage fans also have to dig deep: a medium-sized sign costs no less than 500 dollars, and prices rise to over 1000 dollars. "It depends on the size, the material and the inscription," explains Paul Dvoskin of the MTA. "Location and historical significance of course also matter." The high prices do not deter metro fans and nostalgic commuters. Some 4000 prospective buyers turn up for the sale; the first customer was already standing at the gate of a vacant lot under a railway line in Brooklyn the evening before. A long line of people patiently waits its turn. "I would love to get a sign with Yankee Stadium on it," says Joseph Ciambra to a local medium. Last year he managed to get one with Times Square on it. Austin Celestin hoped to take Lincoln Square home, the station from his youth. Because of the price he had to settle for Columbus Circle, where he also often goes. "I grew up with the metro, I love riding it, so it's nice to be able to take a piece of it home." The MTA collects the pieces throughout the year, when trains are refurbished or stations are renovated. When the first sale was held in 2021, many more people came than expected, says Dvoskin. Nowadays they therefore work with time windows: everyone gets 45 minutes to look around. Dvoskin understands the appeal: "What is more typically New York than the subway?" That the pieces are dirty or covered in graffiti does nothing to diminish that for enthusiasts. On the contrary: "That's exactly what makes it interesting," says customer Nori Juba. "It still smells of the metro, that's what makes it so authentically New York. This is unique worldwide." Among the pieces also wanders director Spike Lee, known for films set in New York such as Do the Right Thing and Inside Man. He finds a sign with Penn Station, the stop for Madison Square Garden, where his beloved Knicks play basketball. "I'm a collector," he replies when asked why he chose this piece. "I don't really take the metro anymore," he admits, but in his youth he did. "And for the record," he adds, he always paid for his rides: "I never jumped the turnstiles." Around 2200 pieces are sold every year. What that yields MTA does not want to say. Dvoskin says the destinations vary: some want a metro bench for their kitchen, others hang a sign in their man cave. As bar decoration the pieces also work well. Ciambra succeeded in getting his Yankees sign. "My day is good again. I had been waiting for this all year. Mission accomplished."

title: Migrant ship capsizes off Djibouti, at least 139 dead
lead: A ship carrying migrants has capsized off the coast of Djibouti in East Africa. At least 139 people have drowned, and another 84 people are missing. The figures come from the International Organization for Migration (IOM), which has staff on the coast of Djibouti. According to the IOM, the accident happened in the night from Thursday to Friday, not far from the coastal town of Obock. The migrant ship had 305 people on board and was on its way from Obock to a port in Yemen. That is a relatively short crossing. Via Yemen, many migrants travel through the wealthy Gulf states on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula. More than eighty people survived the shipwreck. According to the IOM, they all come from Ethiopia, a neighbour of Djibouti. The organization has not disclosed the nationality of the victims. "This tragedy is a painful reminder of the dangers migrants face along this migration route", the IOM writes. Last year, according to the organization, 900 migrants on the route did not reach their destination; they died or went missing. The IOM says that despite the violence in Yemen, many migrants still want to make the crossing from Djibouti. In the past month, the organization counted at least 20,000 migrants who entered the small coastal state from Ethiopia.

title: 'Ukraine won't attack Russian oil installations if Russians stop too'
lead: Ukraine is prepared to stop attacks on Russian oil installations if Russia stops attacking Ukraine's energy supply. That is the response of President Zelensky to President Trump's demand that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries: It is not the first time Zelensky has said this, but it now comes after Trump's attack on him yesterday. The American president said yesterday that it is time Ukraine got a new leader. According to Trump, that should be someone who can make peace with Russia, "something Zelensky never does for some reason". He also said that the war in Ukraine would never have started if he had been US president at the time. "It began thanks to incompetence." Ukrainians decide Zelensky is silent about those statements, but his foreign minister Sybiha says on X: "President Zelensky is leading our nation in a time of war, a war for independence, freedom and dignity. He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide." Trump already let Ukraine down on Friday by concluding an agreement with President Putin on the supply of oil by Russia to the US. Trump hopes that the larger supply will bring down the diesel price in the US. It has doubled since the start of the American-Israeli attack on Iran in February. Trump fears that his party will lose the midterm elections in the US in a few weeks because of this. After the series of attacks on Russian oil installations and storage depots, Ukraine now seems to be targeting data centres. It attacked a data centre of the Russian tech giant Yandex for the third time in four days. Because of the attack on the centre in Vladimir, about 175 kilometres east of Moscow, Yandex users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia cannot use their bank accounts or other online services. "The activities in the data centre have come to a complete standstill", says Yandex. The Yandex data centre in Ryazan, 230 kilometres southeast of Moscow, went completely offline on Thursday after a Ukrainian attack. On Friday the centre in Kaluga, 160 kilometres southwest of Moscow, became partly unusable.

title: Renewed flooding in Nepal, five people missing
lead: Five people have gone missing in a new flood in Nepal. A landslide near the village of Chumnubri sent debris into the Budhi Gandaki river, which led to a flood. According to Nepalese authorities, two women and three men are missing. 49 people were rescued, including a foreigner. So far there have been no reports of fatalities. The flood also caused major damage: at least thirty houses and two suspension bridges were swept away. A construction site of a hydropower plant was also hit, and part of the construction material has been carried away by the river. In these images the force of the water after the landslide is clearly visible: Evacuation Villagers living downstream along the river have been called on to leave their homes and move to safer places. The army, the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> and other rescue workers have been sent to the flood area. The situation is being monitored by helicopter, Nepalese authorities say. The Budhi Gandaki river flows into the Trishuli river. A huge ice avalanche caused a devastating flood there in August. The wave of debris, mud and water swept through the disaster area at speeds of over 180 kilometres per hour. More than 1,300 people died and more than 5,000 people are missing. The Nepalese government now assumes that they are also dead. You can read here how the flood wave in the Trishuli river came about: Weeks after the disaster, the missing were still being searched for, but last week Nepalese prime minister Shah announced that the search would be ended. This caused mixed feelings among the bereaved. Some want the Nepalese government to keep searching for their loved ones, and held demonstrations for that. Others were glad with the decision; they could now apply for a death certificate. According to an estimate by the Nepalese government, the reconstruction of the area will cost well over 4 billion euros.

title: Pope Leo must undergo surgery for lung nodule
lead: Pope Leo XIV has to undergo surgery for a nodule, a kind of small lump on one of his lungs. He said this during the traditional Sunday Angelus prayer. He will be operated on next week. A nodule on the lung does not necessarily have to be serious. The small lump will be examined after the operation. In about five percent of cases it turns out to be cancer, news agency Reuters reports. In the rest of patients it is benign and after the operation there are usually no lasting consequences. The Vatican says that the pope's recovery will take a week. The lump was noticed during a regular health check. The Vatican says nothing further about the health of the 71-year-old pope. The pope's next foreign trip is scheduled for 6 to 17 November. He would then visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. A Vatican spokesperson says nothing about whether or not that trip will go ahead. Pope Leo began his pontificate, as it is called, on 8 May 2025. The American succeeded the late Pope Francis.

title: Deaths in bus crash in Turkey
lead: Eleven people have been confirmed dead in a serious bus crash in Turkey. Another 27 people were injured. The coach crashed on the slip road of a motorway between the cities of Bursa and Izmir, in the west of the country. It is unclear exactly what went wrong. Footage shows the bus lying on its side. Next to it lies a lorry loaded with wood. That lorry has also overturned. The Turkish minister of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> confirms the death toll on X. He says emergency services have been deployed in large numbers to help at the scene of the accident.

title: Round trip via Northern Ice Sea a first for South Korean container ship
lead: In fifty days from South Korea to Europe and back again with a gigantic container ship. That was long impossible, but has now succeeded. The 212-metre-long and 33-metre-wide Panstar Acro left Busan, a port city in South Korea, on 22 August. Now, fifty days later, the ship is back after calling at several European ports, including Rotterdam on 11 September. This was achieved by choosing a route that until a few years ago was impossible for this type of container ship without an icebreaker. The Panstar Acro was the first South Korean container ship to sail there and back via the so-called Northern Sea Route. So along northern Russia, all the way around Russia. Previously still impossible The distance is about half as long as the route through the Suez Canal. That usual route has become more dangerous in recent years due to piracy off the coast of Somalia and recently the attacks by Houthi rebels off the coast of Yemen. The northern route is emerging now due to the consequences of climate change. Until a few years ago it was impossible for large ships to sail so far north. The sea was dangerous due to ice floes, and large parts were only navigable behind an expensive icebreaker that ploughed extremely slowly through the ice. But the Panstar Acro followed the route without help from icebreakers, and the average speed was almost equal to that of the route via the Suez Canal. Regular connection a priority Besides the South Korean ship, in 2026 three other ships also took the direct route between Asia and Europe, all three from China. Last year there was one, according to figures from CHNL, the research and knowledge centre in Norway focused on transport, logistics and economic developments in the High North. The northern route has been designated by the South Korean president as a priority. The country hopes to establish regular connections from 2030. The voyage is therefore celebrated in South Korea as an enormous success. For now the route is only navigable for a few months at the end of summer, when there is little ice. But there are major concerns about the impact on the environment. Critics point out that ships sailing along the ice areas emit soot. If those black particles settle on polar ice and snow, it will melt even faster than it already is. Biologists also fear the consequences for underwater life because ships make a lot of noise, which may have consequences for fish and marine mammals. There are also geopolitical consequences. It is no secret that President Putin is watching the new routes, which partly lead through Russian waters, with great interest. The new shipping may contribute to Russia becoming less isolated in several ways. Especially in the West, that is something not everyone is pleased with. Commercially interesting Finally, the question is when the route will also become commercially interesting. The Panstar Acro had far fewer containers on board than had been calculated in advance. That may indicate that shippers are still hesitant. Higher insurance costs play a role in this, partly due to uncertainty about the reliability of the route. Precisely that reliability is crucial for many companies. That the ship passed through the Northern Ice Sea without problems this time does not mean it will succeed every year. The trial voyage shows that the Northern Sea Route is technically possible, but whether it will also become a full-fledged alternative to the route through the Suez Canal remains to be seen.

title: Utrecht struggles with how to deal with unscrupulous landlords and looks to Rotterdam
lead: Overdue maintenance, discrimination and far too high service charges: landlords in Utrecht regularly break the rules for good landlordship. Yet fines mostly fail to materialise. The municipality is now considering taking stronger action against abuses in the rental sector and is looking to Rotterdam for this. To protect people against, for example, excessive rent or intimidation by the landlord, there is the Good Landlordship Act. This came into force in 2023 and was expanded in 2024. This law stipulates that municipalities may act against rental abuses. Tenants must first report a violation to the municipality. Rent reduced by 350 euros Rotterdam issues fines more quickly than Utrecht for violations. In 2025 Rotterdam imposed 25 fines or orders subject to a penalty payment on landlords. The fines range from 1000 euros to several tens of thousands of euros per violation. That year there were also dozens of investigations into abuses. In that year Rotterdam received 667 reports. The threat of a fine alone seems successful: in many cases the municipality reached agreement with the landlord. After reports of excessive rent, the amount has, according to the municipality of Rotterdam, been reduced by an average of 350 euros. First a warning Utrecht imposed one fine in 2025, RTV Utrecht reports. According to the municipality, this is partly because residents do not always dare to report abuses. In 2025 the municipality received 197 reports. "Many tenants, given the tight housing market, are already glad to have a home and do not want to risk jeopardising their housing situation," the college writes. This municipality further chooses to first give landlords a warning. Not yet decided The municipality will now investigate whether it can adopt Rotterdam's approach. The college thinks fines can be a deterrent and prevent repetition. A decision has not yet been made. The municipality wants to avoid being overturned by the court because the imposed sanction is too severe. The municipality does, however, aim to introduce a rental permit in 2028, whereby the rent can be checked in advance. Furthermore, Utrecht wants to better inform tenants about their rights and about the reporting point where abuses can be reported.

title: Man from Lithuania gets back 24,000 euros of confiscated gambling winnings
lead: A Lithuanian man who was found asleep at the wheel with 24,000 euros last month in Venlo is getting his money back. His claim that he had won the banknotes at the casino turns out to be true, according to an investigation by the Royal Netherlands Marechaussee. After the man won the jackpot on 17 September, he started drinking, L1 Nieuws reports. Driving home was no longer possible. He fell asleep in the car in a car park in Venlo, with the lights and engine on. Drunk: At around 05.00 the marechaussee discovered the car. The Lithuanian was slumped far forward in his seat, with his head in a container of food. Only after the car window had been knocked on firmly several times did he wake up. A breath test showed he had had too much to drink. The man was therefore given a driving ban of twelve hours. Seized: When he had to show his ID card, the marechaussee saw a large number of 100 euro banknotes in his wallet. The man said he had won a large sum of money, but could not prove it. The banknotes were seized. The investigation now shows that the Lithuanian had spoken the truth. He has the full amount back in his possession.

title: Man arrested in Poland for planning an attack on Prime Minister Tusk
lead: A man has been arrested in Poland for preparing an attack on Prime Minister Tusk, reports Marcin Kierwiński, the Polish minister of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>. The identity of the suspect has not been made public. It has also not been disclosed what the background is or how the suspect would have intended to carry out the attack. Tusk thanked the police for their "swift and decisive action". Earlier it became known that Polish security services had convened an emergency meeting after information about a possible attack on Tusk and Minister of Defence Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz. The Polish authorities did not go into detail, but the threat was taken "extremely seriously". The chance that the attack would actually be carried out was described as high. The report of the attack threat came in by email this morning at the state security service, the Ministry of Interior reports. Radical organisation: Polish broadcaster TVN24 says it has seen the content of the email. According to the broadcaster, the person who reported the threat had contact via social media with a radical organisation. That organisation was reportedly looking for people who wanted to carry out attacks with firearms. The person who reported the threat is said to have come into contact with a man with whom he spoke about weapons, hatred of the government and plans for mass murder, TVN24 writes.

title: Saudi Arabia Will 'Strike Back Hard' After Houthi Attack on Riyadh Airport
lead: The direct hit of a Houthi missile on the international airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, is causing great international concern. Because what chain reaction will this set off? Saudi Arabia promises to strike back hard, while fighting is already intense between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen. Director Dania Thafer of research institute Gulf International Forum in Washington expects the Saudis to strike back "quite hard." Speaking to news site Al Jazeera, she says: "I still think the Saudis want de-escalation. They do not want a prolonged escalation. But the Houthis are making it very difficult, because they pose a threat not only to Saudi Arabia's national security but also to international maritime security." A first military response may already have begun. Houthi militias report a Saudi attack on the Sanaa airport, which they control. Saudi Arabia also wants military support from the US in the fight against the Houthis and has been lobbying for it for weeks. In response to the attack, Trump said he is still considering it. Speaking to journalists, he said: "Who knows, we're going to look into it." Twelve dead and at least 300 injured. In the attack on the airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, thirteen people were killed and more than 300 were injured, some of them seriously. Among the dead are four Saudis as well as an American, a Palestinian, and citizens of Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Bangladesh and Sudan. Much remains unclear about the damage. There is little footage, and spreading it carries heavy penalties. One reason is security. The Saudi authorities do not want the enemy to know the ins and outs. Censorship in many Gulf states is strict in any case. Late in the afternoon, the Saudis announced that there had been another attack on the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday. A projectile reportedly struck the passenger terminal again. A number of people were reportedly injured. Beyond that, little is known. Saudi Arabia has also not yet said who might be behind it. Today, the international airport in Riyadh is in any case closed until 21:00.
