A fire broke out on board, the Singapore maritime service reports. No one was injured, and the 21 crew members have been evacuated. The second ship, Cape Dao, which sailed under the flag of Antigua and Barbuda, sank near Oman. That ship had already been hit by a projectile on 23 September, when one crew member died. The other people on board were, according to maritime sources, evacuated immediately after the impact. Iranian state television has shown footage of both ships: That a ship sinks after an attack in the waterway is rare. The last time a ship sank in the area was in March, according to the International Maritime Organization (IMO). The container ship Safeen Prestige, sailing under the Maltese flag, was hit by a projectile on 4 March and later sank in the waterway. In total, three ships have sunk since the American-Israeli attacks on Iran, which began at the end of February. Attacks stepped up Earlier, the British Financial Times wrote that Iran has stepped up attacks on ships in and around the Strait of Hormuz this month. It would be the largest series of attacks since the start of the war. Last Sunday, according to the newspaper, six ships were attacked. In the first eleven days of October, Iran hit 24 ships in total. Iran states that it has stepped up the attacks in response to the American blockade of Iranian ports and the stricter sanctions imposed on the country last month.

title: Polish judge sworn in again without president present, protests at court
lead: The political conflict over the independence of the Polish judiciary has escalated with the appointment of Maciej Berek as a judge of the Constitutional Court. Berek took the oath this morning without President Nawrocki being present. The appointment led to protests outside the court in the capital, Warsaw. The swearing-in of Berek is part of a years-long political struggle over the independence of the Polish judiciary. The Polish parliament, where the governing coalition of pro-European, liberal Prime Minister Tusk has a majority, elects the judges of the Constitutional Court, one of the country's most important judicial bodies. During Berek's swearing-in, supporters of the right-conservative opposition party Law and Justice (PiS) demonstrated. Clashes with police broke out and three people were arrested, Polish media write. Veto right The Constitutional Court, which consists of fifteen judges, assesses whether laws comply with the Polish constitution. New judges are elected by parliament, but by law must take the oath before the president. The Polish president, the conservative nationalist Nawrocki, is seen as a political opponent of Tusk and refuses to swear in Berek. As president, he has a veto and can thereby block laws. In his view, Berek does not meet the legal requirements; he argues that Berek has not worked in the legal world long enough to qualify for the appointment. Berek disputes this. Nawrocki also objects to his political background. Berek was a minister in Tusk's cabinet until August, and Tusk had earlier called him his "right hand". His appointment led to criticism not only from the opposition but also within Tusk's own governing coalition. At his inauguration in 2023, Tusk promised to end political appointments in the judiciary. Because Nawrocki did not want to receive him, Berek took the oath in parliament without the president present. He is now the fifth judge to do so in this way. Of the eight judges parliament has elected this year, Nawrocki has sworn in only three. The chairman of the court, Bogdan Swieczkowski, who is linked to PiS, refuses to let Berek start work as a judge. He does not recognize the swearing-in. The other four judges who were not sworn in by Nawrocki are also not allowed to work. When they arrived at the court in April, they got no further than the lobby of the building and were stopped. Yesterday, the Venice Commission, an advisory body of the Council of Europe, ruled that the president must swear in new judges without delay. If he refuses, they may, according to the commission, also take the oath without his presence. This is an advice, which the president is not obliged to follow. Years-long struggle The struggle over the Constitutional Court has been going on for years. Under the previous PiS government, which was in power from 2015 to 2023, far-reaching political influence was exercised over the judiciary. For example, party loyalists were appointed to the Constitutional Court in a controversial manner. This led to a deeply escalating conflict with Brussels. The European Commission blocked billions of euros in subsidies for Poland. After Tusk took office, the way was cleared again for European funds worth 137 billion euros, because his government had taken steps to restore the rule of law. Since then, various reforms have been carried out, but major changes have not followed. This is partly because Nawrocki and his predecessor can block reforms through the veto. 'Restoring the legal order' Prime Minister Tusk promised today that he will restore the legal order. In his view, Poland has been functioning for far too long without a properly elected constitutional court. "We will restore the legal order and the constitution with the means the state has at its disposal," he said.

title: Prisoner (34) freed by masked men during doctor's visit in Essen
lead: In the German city of Essen, a prisoner has escaped during a doctor's visit. The 34-year-old German prisoner was freed by two masked men who overpowered two prison guards. Around 12:45 PM, the two guards were attacked and tied up in the hallway of the building. According to the German news agency DPA, one of the guards drew his service weapon during this, but it was knocked out of his hand. The prisoner then fled on an electric scooter. His accomplices fled separately from each other in other directions. Organized crime The man was in pretrial detention on suspicion of drug offenses and serious assault. He is linked to organized crime. The police have launched a large search for the three men and have distributed a photo of the escaped prisoner. Involvement of others is not ruled out. The police warn people not to approach the man themselves, as he may be armed. Dummy grenade During the search, a suspicious object resembling a hand grenade was found a few hundred meters from the doctor's practice. An explosives disposal service examined the object and it turned out to be a wooden dummy grenade. It is still unclear whether the object has anything to do with the escape.

title: Designer Christien Meindertsma is the first winner of the Paul Deiters Prize
lead: Designer Christien Meindertsma is the first winner of a new art award given every three years, the Paul Deiters Prize. According to the foundation behind the prize, Stichting Stokroos, Meindertsma creates "distinctive work" in which art, design, research, materials and social issues come together. The prize comes with an amount of 120,000 euros: 60,000 euros as a cash prize and the same amount for the development of new work. In addition, the winner may show work in a museum. In Meindertsma's case, this is at an exhibition at the Kunstmuseum in The Hague next year. Flax and wool. Meindertsma has been working as a designer for about twenty years. She likes to work with sustainable products such as flax and wool. She also focuses on research projects, such as PIG 05049 , in which she investigated which products can be made from one pig, and Flax Project , in which she searched for new uses for flax. Another project is the development of Wobot: a robot that can felt wool three-dimensionally. Stichting Stokroos calls Meindertsma a pioneer in contextual design. "She looks not only at what something looks like, but mainly at where it comes from, how it is made, and what stories and systems lie behind it. It is precisely this combination of designing, researching and social context that makes her work so innovative and relevant." "I want to find solutions for polluting systems with my work and gain more influence over the whole process," says Meindertsma in the same press release. "I am fascinated by the materials we have around us, such as wool, linen and willow twigs, and how much knowledge and history is hidden in them." Paul Deiters. The new art prize is named after businessman and art lover Paul Deiters (1952-2017), founder of Stichting Stokroos. This foundation wants to support visual artists, designers and craftspeople in their development and help talents on their way.

title: Found aircraft wreck in Dronten turns out to be British WWII bomber
lead: After extensive research, the municipality of Dronten has established that the aircraft remains found in a wood are from a British bomber shot down during the Second World War. The remains of the old aircraft were discovered four years ago during trench works in the Van Veldhuizenbos in Dronten. Omroep <entity id="org:provincie-flevoland">Flevoland</entity> reports that researchers have established that the remains found are part of an Avro Lancaster Mk III JB120 LQ-D that was shot down over the IJsselmeer on the night of 27 to 28 September 1943. The aircraft was part of the Canadian 405 Pathfinder Squadron, which was stationed at an airfield near the English city of Cambridge. Failure That night the Lancaster flew together with almost 700 other aircraft towards Germany to bomb the city of Hannover. "However, this attack was a failure", the municipality of Dronten writes. "The scouting Pathfinders had used incorrect wind calculations, so that most of the target markers had blown away. As a result the bombs did not land on Hannover, but in an open field a few kilometres further on and on surrounding villages." The Lancaster did not reach Hannover. At 22.10 hours the aircraft was shot down on the way there by a German night fighter and crashed into the IJsselmeer, at the spot where the Van Veldhuizenbos now lies. The seven-member crew consisted of four Canadians, an Australian, a Scot and a Briton. Their bodies were never found. In 1959, however, remains were found in the area. These were buried at the military cemetery Jonkerbos in <entity id="org:gemeente-nijmegen">Nijmegen</entity>. During the recovery of the Lancaster parts, human remains were again found. Whether these come from the seven crew members is still being investigated by the Bergings- en Identificatiedienst of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-defensie">Defensie</entity>. Mayor <entity id="person:jean-paul-gebben">Jean Paul Gebben</entity> of Dronten calls the identification of the aircraft of great historical value. "Behind every aircraft wreck lies a human story", he says. According to him, the seven men who have been missing since 1943 thereby regain a place in the history of the municipality. Unique identification number To establish which aircraft it was, the wreck was recovered in November 2025. For four weeks specialists searched for parts. This had to be done with extreme care, because there was also ammunition lying there, which could explode. During the work large quantities of soil were excavated and various aircraft parts were found. Ultimately, unique identification numbers on two pieces of aluminium proved decisive. It turned out to be the same Lancaster from which a gun turret had previously been found in the area. 5500 aircraft lost Part of the recovered wreckage will be lent to museums and foundations, so that the story of the Lancaster and its crew can be retold. It is estimated that around 5500 aircraft were lost over the Netherlands during the Second World War. A maximum of three aircraft recoveries are carried out each year. The recovery in Dronten ultimately cost well over 960.000 euros. Most of the costs were paid by the national government. Newsletter Second World War Interested in the Second World War? Subscribe to our newsletter here.

title: Unrest in Amsterdam neighborhood Floradorp, three arrests
lead: In the Amsterdam neighborhood of Floradorp it was restless this evening. The mobile unit was deployed after residents set fires and turned against emergency workers. Three people have been arrested for vandalism, including two minors. The unrest reportedly followed a letter from <entity id="person:femke-halsema">burgemeester Halsema</entity> rejecting an alternative plan for a bonfire. At the start of the evening, a fire was set in Sneeuwbalstraat in <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity>-Noord. People had piled up junk in this street and set it alight. According to the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>, it became restless when the fire brigade arrived to put out the fire. Officers supported firefighters in fighting the fire. "When residents turned against them, they had to leave for their own safety," says a police spokesperson. Stones and fireworks were thrown at emergency workers. The calm has now returned to the neighborhood. Alternative bonfire. Earlier in the day, residents of Floradorp received a letter from mayor Halsema in which their alternative plan for the traditional New Year's bonfire is rejected. The neighborhood wanted a smaller fire in an open container, but according to the fire brigade, an open fire in a residential area is too dangerous to allow. Halsema has adopted this advice. At the end of last year, it was also restless in Floradorp after mayor Halsema banned the traditional bonfire because of safety risks. Fires were set repeatedly at that time, and the ME also intervened several times.

title: Books by Sally Rooney pulled from sale in UK over support for Palestine Action
lead: The books of Irish bestselling author Sally Rooney are being pulled from sale in the United Kingdom because of her support for the British pro-Palestinian action group Palestine Action. Her publisher Faber & Faber has therefore decided to no longer print new editions of her books. After the British cabinet listed Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation last year, support for that action group was also banned. The 35-year-old author, known for the books Normale mensen, Gesprekken met vrienden, Prachtige wereld, waar ben je? and Intermezzo, then told The Irish Times that she wants to keep using the proceeds from her books to support Palestine Action. Rooney's British publisher, Faber & Faber, reports that the ban on the action group has meant that no royalties can be paid out to Rooney. "Selling an author's work and being unable to pass on the income is an unacceptable situation for a publisher," the publisher says. Rooney says she fully stands behind the consequences of her support for Palestine Action. Millions of books sold. Rooney debuted in 2017 with her book Gesprekken met vrienden, which became a twelve-part television series in 2022. She only truly broke through with her second novel, Normale mensen. That book also became a series, with Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones in the lead roles. Rooney has sold more than six million books, the British broadcaster BBC reports. More than two million copies sold in the United Kingdom.

title: US states find ChatGPT harmful to children and file lawsuit
lead: Eight American states are filing a lawsuit against technology company OpenAI. Among others, the states of Iowa, Kansas and Arizona accuse the American company of having misled users about the safety of the popular chatbot ChatGPT. It is said to have encouraged people to self-harm and to commit violence against others. According to the states, OpenAI says that ChatGPT is a safe tool while in reality that is not the case, and the chatbot has been designed so that it quickly wins users' trust. "OpenAI is putting children in danger and lying to residents of Iowa," said prosecutor Brenna Bird of Iowa. "OpenAI claims that ChatGPT is safe while it gives dangerous medical advice, encourages people to hurt others and incites people to suicide." And all of this happens while, according to Bird, ChatGPT pretends to be their imaginary friend. Fines The eight states demand that OpenAI be forced to adjust ChatGPT. Among other things, the states want the tech company to stop developing AI models that can improve themselves, unless it can guarantee that those models are aligned with human values. The states also demand fines. Last month the Canadian province of British Columbia sued OpenAI over the company's role in a fatal shooting. Earlier this year an 18-year-old shot eight people dead in the province, including her mother and stepbrother. Afterwards she took her own life. The shooter planned the shooting with the help of ChatGPT, but despite warning signs the police were not called in. Her account was deactivated, but she was able to create a new account and continue planning the shooting. Need help? Are you thinking of suicide or worried about someone? Talking helps. You can do this 24/7, free and anonymously via the chat at www.113.nl or by phone on 113 or 0800-0113.

title: Kandinsky looted by Nazis sold at auction for nearly 32 million euros
lead: The work Das bunte Leben by the famous Russian-French expressionist Wassily Kandinsky was sold at a Christie's auction in London for 27 million pounds (nearly 32 million euros). In 2023 the German public prosecutor's office classified the painting as looted art and returned it to the heirs of the Jewish couple Lewenstein. Emanuel and Hedwig Lewenstein lived in the last century in <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity> and had a sewing machine factory on the Dam. The family had a large art collection, including works by Jan Toorop, Jozef Israëls and Jean Metzinger. Kandinsky made the auctioned work Das bunte Leben (the colorful life) in 1907 in Paris, where he was living at the time with his lover Gabriele Münter, also an artist. Emanuel and Hedwig Lewenstein bought the colorful painting in 1927. German occupation. Shortly after the start of the German occupation of the Netherlands, the work was auctioned and came into the hands of the Jewish art collector Sal Slijper. His family sold the work to the Bayerische Landesbank, which transferred it on permanent loan to the Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus, a museum in Munich. The work was on display there for decades. Research shows that a museum employee had the work (130x 162 cm) brought to the auction house in 1940 by a courier on the orders of an unknown person, where it was then offered for sale. According to the researchers, there are numerous indications that the Nazis had seized the painting. After the war, the children of the Lewenstein couple did everything they could to trace their parents' looted collection. The German bank returned the Kandinsky work to the heirs in 2023. Just over 60 million euros: In 2023 the heirs of the sewing machine manufacturer had already sold Kandinsky's Bild mit Häusern for just over 60 million euros. That painting was returned after a long-running dispute with the municipality of Amsterdam. Until February 2022 the painting hung in the permanent exhibition space of the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam.

lead: Good morning! title: Busy election year adds extra pressure to European budget negotiations
lead: The leaders of the EU countries are speaking today in Brussels about a new European budget, high energy prices and new financial support for Ukraine. The discussion is under pressure from upcoming elections in four of the five largest EU countries, which could significantly shake up the balance of power within the EU in the coming year. The Spaniards (2026), French, Poles and Italians (2027) will go to the polls between now and the end of 2027. Especially the French presidential elections in April could strongly influence the negotiations on the European budget for the next seven years. In addition, they may have consequences for financial support to Ukraine. Campaign in Brussels In the French polls, the radical-right party Rassemblement National of Marine Le Pen is in the lead. Le Pen argues that France should contribute billions less to the European Union. Moreover, she sees no room for financial support to Ukraine. Ukraine is expected to fall short by tens of billions of euros next year to cover military and social costs, but the money is first needed in France, Le Pen believes, because her country is struggling with an enormous national debt. She makes Ukraine and the negotiations on the European budget part of her election campaign. For that reason she appeared yesterday, on the eve of the summit with EU leaders, at a press conference in a hotel in central Brussels. Her message to European journalists: the EU could look very different in a year. With much more influence from parties that would most like to sharply restrict the power of the EU. Tough negotiation So Le Pen hopes that her Spanish ally, the radical-right Vox, will manage to gain a place in a new Spanish government. Vox is now third in the polls. Le Pen's party colleague, Jordan Bardella, visited Santiago Abascal, the parliamentary leader of Vox in Spain, this week to express his support. The French believe that a good result for Vox in November could set the tone for the rest of the election year. Besides the votes in Spain, France, Italy and Poland, there are also elections in Estonia, Finland and Greece, among others. With her visit to the Belgian capital, Le Pen literally brings the French elections to Brussels. Although as a presidential candidate she may not sit in on the summit of EU leaders, they will certainly feel her presence. Especially in the discussion about a new budget for 2028 through 2034. Early deadline The heads of government and state of the 27 EU countries hope to come somewhat closer to an agreement today on how much money they want to spend in the coming years and on what. That discussion is so far extremely difficult. That is not unusual. Every seven years, countries that pay more money to the EU than they receive, such as Germany and the Netherlands, mainly want to cut costs. Opposing them is a large group of countries that would like to see a larger European budget. This often leads to negotiations that continue until the very last moment, because all countries ultimately have to agree. But this year European Council president Antonio Costa, the man who must steer the talks between the European leaders in the right direction, aims for an agreement still in 2026, a year before the budget is due to take effect in 2028. Costa hopes in this way to prevent all elections next year, and especially the French one, from completely derailing the negotiations. 'Democratic scandal' That early deadline seems too ambitious. So far the countries are not getting closer to an agreement. Moreover, not everyone is in a hurry. "We will not sign an agreement that is not favourable, just to meet the deadline," Italian prime minister Meloni said yesterday. Meanwhile Le Pen is trying to increase pressure on the current French president Macron not to conclude an agreement before his departure. That would, in her view, be a 'democratic scandal', just before the elections. It puts Macron in a difficult position in his final months as president: try to reach an agreement with his 26 colleagues in the coming months, with the risk that such a compromise plays into the hands of political opponents. Or wait, with the possible result that his successor torpedoes the budget negotiations.

title: Bridge between North Korea and China opens after twelve years of delay
lead: After a delay of twelve years, China and North Korea have put into use a bridge over a border river between the two countries. The New Yalu River Bridge connects the Chinese city of Dandong with Sinuiju on the other side. The bridge was already largely completed in 2014, but North Korea stalled its connection to the road network. The relationship between North Korea and China cooled in the years after that because of North Korea's nuclear weapons program. Now that both countries are tightening their ties again, the time was ripe to open the bridge. Another, older bridge already crosses the Yalu. It handles more than 70 percent of trade between the two countries and was therefore the most important border crossing between them. The new bridge is 3 kilometers long and has four lanes. Even before the bridge officially opened, trucks lined up on the Chinese side of the border to be the first to cross it. China is still the most important trading partner for North Korea, but the regime in Pyongyang has recently also sought more connection with Russia. For example, trade and tourism were stepped up, and North Korea sent soldiers to fight against Ukraine. Last month North Korea also opened a new land route to Russia, with a bridge over the Tumen River.

title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil sector, Russia reports attack on refinery
lead: Ukraine has resumed attacks on Russia's energy sector after three days of pause. President Zelensky announced in an interview with the British newspaper Financial Times that the temporary halt to bombardments is officially over. Overnight, according to Russian authorities, a drone attack was already carried out on an oil refinery in the Ryazan region, in the west of the country. "The attack pause is over," Zelensky told the Financial Times. "I told the army that after people were killed again in Russian attacks." Zelensky made this decision because the Kremlin was already not adhering to the ceasefire that Trump suddenly announced last Sunday. The American president said then that Russia and Ukraine would spare each other's energy sector in attacks, as part of a diesel deal he had concluded with the Kremlin. Russian violations: Although he had not been consulted in advance, Zelensky said he would respect the ceasefire, as long as Russia also adhered to it. After Russia deployed 39 ballistic missiles and 120 drones in the night from Tuesday to Wednesday, Zelensky's patience ran out. He added that he had not yet discussed the decision with President Trump. "If they do that, how long can we postpone attacks on Russian refineries?" he asked rhetorically. "The first day was only a petrol station and some fuel infrastructure, and the second day not much either, but at night they immediately attacked the important energy infrastructure again, especially in Kyiv." Yesterday more than half a million Ukrainians were without power due to ongoing large-scale Russian attacks on both power plants and crucial infrastructure in Ukraine. In the first Ukrainian attack on the Russian oil sector since Sunday, according to the governor of Ryazan no one was killed, but emergency services had to turn out for a fire. Putin's war chest: The ceasefire that Trump announced on his own initiative was part of the diesel deal the American president concluded with the Kremlin. Trump hopes that through the direct delivery of initially 300,000 tonnes of Russian diesel to the US he can lower fuel prices for Americans. Essential to this is that Ukraine stops drone attacks deep into Russia on oil refineries. For Ukraine this form of warfare is extremely important: it hits the Russian economy hard and thereby Putin's war chest. In large parts of the country there are major fuel shortages and rationing has been introduced. Probably to increase pressure on Ukraine, the country was yesterday, without prior warning, also confronted with problems with the military arm of Starlink, the satellite system of American billionaire Elon Musk that is indispensable to the Ukrainian army for advanced drone operations. According to the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence, the connection with the drones falters when they fly faster than 160 kilometres per hour, while high speed is crucial in attacks. Problems with intelligence: Musk responded by stating that Starlink's "restrictions on speed or use are determined by the American military and ultimately by the President of the United States". The imposed limit on the system also makes it harder for Ukraine to intercept Russian drones and missiles, which can reach speeds up to 500 kilometres per hour. In the interview with the Financial Times Zelensky says he does not believe there was a malfunction. "It was not a technical problem, it was deliberate," he says. There are also problems regarding the intelligence the Americans share with Ukraine. Although Trump claims it still shares intelligence with Kyiv, Zelensky said that earlier this week it had not received information about Russian attacks on Kyiv. During a visit to London, Zelensky said yesterday: "It is regrettable that we have problems with Starlink and with intelligence. These are surprises you do not expect when you are truly partners." According to several media, Trump has threatened that the US will no longer share information about Russian missile launches if Ukraine attacks Russian oil installations.

title: Several dead in heavy rainfall in Istanbul, 14-year-old boy electrocuted
lead: Heavy flooding in the Turkish city of Istanbul has claimed at least two lives. That is what several Turkish news channels report. A 14-year-old boy died after stepping into a puddle of water and being electrocuted as a result. The child collapsed and lost consciousness. He was taken to hospital, but died there. Turkish authorities have launched an investigation into the incident in the Fatih district. In addition, a 34-year-old man died after being swept away by the water and then falling with his head onto the pavement. He too eventually died in hospital. Thousands of reports: The flooding is the result of heavy rainfall, according to local authorities the worst since 1985. In some parts of the city, according to the Turkish meteorological service, 242 millimetres of rain have fallen so far. The emergency services have received nearly 7000 reports of nuisance. Footage shows cars floating through the streets. And due to landslides, large cracks have appeared in the roads and many cars have been stranded: Furthermore, tunnels and metro stations have been flooded. Schools and government buildings remain closed due to the extreme weather. City authorities call on people to stay indoors and to leave their homes only if it is really unavoidable.

title: Lawyer or just a jurist? New White House spokesperson immediately under fire
lead: The new White House spokesperson is under fire because she appears to have wrongly embellished her CV. Katie Zacharia said she was qualified to work as a lawyer, but there is no evidence for that. Zacharia herself considers it mainly a misunderstanding, but critics argue that the credibility of the face of the White House is at stake. Precisely in her role, the right wording matters. The 41-year-old political commentator Zacharia was appointed this weekend as the new spokesperson for President Trump. At her appointment, the president said that for her political activities she had built a career as a lawyer, attorney. She also said she had served as general counsel at a company, which also requires extra papers. Bar exam Practicing as a lawyer, a protected profession, requires an extra exam after law school, the bar exam. Journalists who checked her qualifications could find no evidence that Zacharia ever passed it. She once did attempt it, but unsuccessfully. Zacharia herself says that after her law studies she has always used the title jurist, lawyer. When journalists asked where she had taken her bar exam, she did answer that it was "when she moved to China". Zacharia worked between 2011 and 2013 for a law firm in Beijing. However, the Chinese bar exam is not accessible to foreigners, so it is impossible for them to work as a lawyer there. Asked for an explanation, Zacharia told The New York Times that she had misunderstood the question because the presidential helicopter was already running. She believed the question had been where she went after her studies. There was indeed a lot of noise when the question was asked: Although Zacharia mainly considers this legal hair-splitting, an interest group has filed a complaint. In California it is indeed illegal to call yourself a lawyer without the proper credentials. After returning from China, Zacharia worked, among other things, as a legal adviser to a conservative political lobby group. This year she worked for a few months as a communications adviser for the company that runs Trump's Truth Social network, and she was deputy press secretary for the Department of Homeland Security. Commentators call that remarkably little relevant experience for the most important mouthpiece of the White House. During her years as a commentator, Zacharia advocated strongly right-wing policies, such as suspending constitutional rights to combat illegal immigration. She also spread conspiracy theories that electoral fraud cost Trump the 2020 elections and that Democrats and Hollywood stars are murderous paedophiles. A difficult first day American media wrote scornfully about Zacharia's first press conference this week. She spent the quarter hour she allotted for it mainly praising Trump's policies. Only three journalists were allowed to ask questions, all from media that are friendly to Trump. According to commentators, Zacharia came across as nervous, and the fact that she made heavy use of her notes suggested she was not yet well versed in the subject. During the press conference she also made a slip and called her husband "my president". Choosing an inexperienced spokesperson is striking in this period, just before next month's midterm elections. In those elections she must try to convey Trump's positions as effectively as possible at a time when the president is struggling with low approval ratings. It did not bother President Trump. Asked how he thought her first working day had gone, his answer was: "I thought she was very good".

title: 57 people arrested in Croatia after clash between Ajax and Hajduk Split fans
lead: In the Croatian city of Split, 57 people were arrested overnight by the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> after a clash between fans of football clubs Ajax and Hajduk Split. The clubs play each other tonight in the Conference League. The police had to intervene to prevent hundreds of troublemakers from coming to blows in the city centre, Croatian media report. It involved about 200 Ajax supporters and 300 Torcida Split (fanatical fans of Hajduk Split). About 100 officers were deployed, but reinforcements arrived quickly. It is not clear whether Dutch fans were also arrested. Calm was restored after fifteen minutes, the police say. No one was injured. Days of unrest. The city has been restless for days leading up to the match. In total, over 150 fans have been arrested in the past two nights. The night before last, eighteen Ajax supporters were picked up. They reportedly also had weapons with them, Croatian media write. There have been five incidents so far, says Srdarević, head of the local police. In four cases, it involved confrontations between supporters of the two clubs, and in two of those, Dutch nationals were slightly injured. A criminal investigation into the perpetrators is underway. "We were aware that this would be a major challenge," says the police chief, "given the large number of fans of both clubs, especially those who misbehave". Additional police deployment. The police have been prepared for incidents around the match since last Tuesday up to and including tomorrow evening. Tonight 600 officers are being deployed in the city, the stadium and the area around the stadium. Other police forces are assisting. The police may also detain people who misbehave for two hours today, which is normally not allowed but is permitted on match days. The city expects 1900 supporters from the Netherlands. Tickets for away supporters are sold out.

title: Over 30 children killed when school collapses in Pakistan
lead: Dozens of children and a teacher have died after the roof of a school in Pakistan collapsed, Pakistani media report. Dozens of pupils were also injured. The death toll has now risen to 35, and most of the victims are between 6 and 14 years old. A hospital spokesperson says most of the injured children can go home, but at least three children have been admitted with serious head injuries. Rescue workers have freed dozens of children from under the rubble, and the rescue mission has now ended. The roof of the two-storey private school in Peshawar in northwest Pakistan suddenly gave way. The pupils were in their classrooms at the time of the collapse. According to a police officer on site, the structure of the building was weak. "The roof was too heavy for the weak structure, causing the building to collapse." Thorough investigation promised. Pakistani President Zardari is deeply shocked by the incident, he writes on X. "May Almighty Allah grant the victims a high place in Paradise and give the bereaved the courage and strength to bear this irreparable loss." Zardari says he wants a thorough investigation into the cause, to prevent similar incidents in the future. It is not the first time a school building has collapsed in Pakistan. In June, at least fourteen pupils died when the roof of a school in Lahore collapsed. The victims were between 5 and 16 years old.

title: 'Ukraine has full access to the military branch of Starlink again'
lead: The Ukrainian army has access again to Starshield, the military branch of the American satellite network Starlink. This is reported by news agency Reuters, based on a source within the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence. The Kyiv Independent also writes that the connection has now been restored, although the Ukrainian newspaper says it is not certain whether speed limits for drones still apply. "The Starshield service has now been restored and remains operational," said the newspaper's source. There had been problems since yesterday with the system of American tech billionaire Elon Musk. SpaceX, the parent company of Starlink and Starshield, suddenly introduced limits without any prior warning, causing Ukrainian drones to falter when they flew faster than 160 kilometres per hour, which made the Ukrainian army vulnerable. Attacks deep in Russia: To be able to defend its own airspace and carry out attacks deep inside Russia, the drones must in fact be able to fly many times faster, in some cases up to 500 kilometres per hour. The system is also essential for the military communications of the top of the Ukrainian army. Reuters' source says it is still being investigated what caused the disruption. Ukrainian President Zelensky told the British newspaper Financial Times that he does not believe a technical fault caused the problems. "It was not a technical problem, it was deliberate." Musk says he is in any case not to blame. Restrictions on speed or use are, according to him, determined by the American military "and ultimately by the President of the United States," he wrote on social media. First attack in days: Last night Ukraine carried out an attack on a Russian oil refinery for the first time in days. It had temporarily stopped doing so, at the request of US President Trump, since Sunday. Zelensky no longer saw any point in the partial truce because Russia kept attacking the energy sector in Ukraine. The Ukrainian navy also reports that last night, in an attack on the Borisoglebsk military airfield in the southwest of Russia, it hit six Russian bombers. No drones were used for this; missiles were fired from warships.

title: Can Russia still export diesel after years of attacks on refineries?
lead: On Friday, US President Trump announced a deal with Russia that is to bring millions of barrels of diesel onto the world market. But can Russia actually deliver that diesel now that Ukrainian President Zelensky says he is resuming attacks on Russian energy targets? Russia makes diesel by converting crude oil into diesel in refineries. Ukraine is trying to shut down those refineries with drone attacks, just as Russia does to the energy infrastructure in Ukraine. Since the war began, refining capacity in Russia has declined considerably, according to a report by The Oxford Institute for Energy Studies. Shortly after the Russian invasion in February 2022, Ukraine began retaliatory attacks on the oil and gas infrastructure in Russia. Recently the pace was stepped up. In the first half of 2026, 22 of the 34 refineries in Russia were attacked. Analysts estimate that Russia's refining capacity has fallen by 30 percent compared with before the war. Russia is the second-largest diesel exporter in the world, after the United States. Normally the country has a surplus of diesel, but as a result of the damaged refineries a shortage of oil products arose in Russia itself. The Kremlin therefore decided to ban exports of oil products such as petrol and, more recently, diesel too. Data from data provider Kpler show that diesel exports came to a complete standstill in September, whereas a year earlier they had still been between 1.5 and 2.5 million tonnes per month. That raises the question of whether President Putin can actually deliver on the diesel deal. Under the agreement, Russia would deliver 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US this month, rising later in the year to as much as 3 million tonnes, roughly 21 million barrels. Whether that will succeed depends, according to Kpler analyst Ivan Rjabov, on how hard the refineries in Russia are hit in the coming period. Ukraine recently appears to be focusing its attacks more on data centres than on oil infrastructure. Rjabov thinks diesel exports will certainly get going again, at least at the start. "The volume of the first delivery is far below what Russia exported before the war, so they can certainly deliver that." But whether that also applies to the larger deliveries later this year remains to be seen, according to Rjabov. Summer diesel: Russia still has some 'summer diesel' in storage. That is diesel without anti-freeze additive. "I think they would really like to be rid of that," says Lucia van Geuns, energy expert at The Hague Centre for Strategic Studies. Russia switches from summer to winter diesel in the autumn, so the summer diesel is released. Even so, exporting it is not that easy yet. Van Geuns stresses that ports also play an important role in the ability to export. "Russia ships oil and oil products via the Black and Baltic Seas, but there you see Ukraine still carrying out attacks," said van Geuns. The diesel deal is meeting resistance from all sides because it would finance Putin's state coffers. Revenues from oil and gas are one of the most important sources of income for Russia. On average the sector accounts for a fifth of the total size of the Russian economy. "Oil is the cash cow for the country," says Morena Skalamera, assistant professor of Russian studies at Leiden University. "Other countries such as China, Turkey and India still buy a lot of oil from Russia." Filling the state coffers: The loss of exports of oil and oil products in 2026 has been fully offset by higher oil prices as a result of the Iran war, researchers from the above-mentioned report by The Oxford Institute for Energy Studies say. "Russia is profiting enormously from geopolitical turmoil," says Skalamera. That suggests the Russian war economy is still running at full tilt. "In the long term the attacks will certainly have an impact on the Russian economy, but it is still far from collapsing." The diesel deal with Trump appears mainly to be a political victory for Putin. The amount is small, but it does go directly to financing the war against Ukraine. Consumers should not expect lower prices at the pump soon either, says energy expert Van Geuns. "Because it concerns only a small amount of diesel at a global level, the price at the pump will not fall quickly."

title: Tech shares fall on AI doubts, ASML deep in the red
lead: On the stock exchanges in Europe and Asia, tech and AI shares are deep in the red today. On the Amsterdam exchange, the ASML share was at one point down 6.7 percent compared with yesterday's closing price. ASML makes machines that produce computer chips and is the global market leader in the most advanced chips for AI applications. In recent months, stock markets had been breaking record after record, partly due to optimism about tech companies and the development of artificial intelligence. Tech companies are investing many billions in the further development of AI and the construction of data centres. Expensive investments Investors now seem to be wondering how much profit all those billions invested in AI will generate, at a time when interest rates are high and financing all those investments is therefore relatively expensive. Other Dutch tech shares are also losing value. For example, Advanced Semiconductor Materials (ASM) is down around 8 percent and BE Semiconductor Industries (BESI) is down more than 5 percent. Laura van Megen, correspondent for China and East Asia: "Across East Asia, stock markets are turning red because investors are selling their shares in computer chip-related companies. The South Korean stock index saw the biggest fall, dropping 7.57 percent. Stock markets in China, Japan, Taiwan and Hong Kong also closed in the red. The South Korean market is seen as the world's most volatile, with many rapid rises and falls. The AI craze only amplifies that. The two big chipmakers, Samsung and SK Hynix, have profited greatly recently, because their memory chips are in high demand from AI companies. But today both ended about 10 percent in the red. Because those two together account for nearly 20 percent of the South Korean economy, it rippled through the entire market. Taiwan also saw one of its heaviest stock market falls ever, of 3.41 percent. There too the tech sector makes up a large part of the economy, which makes the island vulnerable at moments like this. The world's largest chipmaker, TSMC, also published a profit increase of nearly 70 percent today. Nevertheless, TSMC ended two percent in the red. TSMC supplies chips to tech companies such as Apple and Nvidia." What is notable is that the losses on the Amsterdam exchange are concentrated in tech shares. The AEX index is, after all, showing a relatively small loss of 0.85 percent.

title: Major fire destroys warehouse in Berkel en Rodenrijs, fire possibly arson
lead: A car dealership was completely destroyed by a fire in Berkel en Rodenrijs. No one was injured. A warehouse where the company was located has burned out completely. The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> is investigating whether there was arson. In the same building on Noordseindeweg there was also a fire two years ago. At that time a car containing the body of a 20-year-old man was found in the warehouse, along with items for producing drugs. According to the police, no "unusual circumstances" were found in the warehouse this time. The fire broke out last night around 03.00 hours. According to the police, the flames quickly spread and a lot of smoke was released. Around 05.30 hours the fire brigade declared the fire under control. "They had just rebuilt it all. But they can do that again now," says a spokesperson for the safety region about the farm to the regional broadcaster Rijnmond. Also explosions. Whether there is a link with the earlier fire is not yet clear, but that will be investigated as soon as possible. In the course of the day the police will carry out further research into how this fire could have started. "A fully blazing fire in the middle of the night raises questions," said the spokesperson of the safety region. According to the police, there were also several explosions in the region last night: two in Rotterdam, one in Dordrecht and a fourth in Berkel en Rodenrijs. That last explosion was at a business premises on Industrieweg, about five kilometres from the building where the fire raged. No one was injured, but the explosions did cause damage. The police say there are so far no indications that there is a link between last night's explosions and the large fire at the warehouse, "but this will also be looked into further in the investigation".

title: Police find 50 heavy explosives in basement storage unit under flat in Utrecht
lead: Police have found fifty heavy fireworks bombs in a basement storage unit in the Utrecht neighbourhood of Overvecht. The owner, a 55-year-old man, has been arrested. Officers found the explosives the day before yesterday during an inspection with the municipality in a flat on the Tigrisdreef. They are Cobra 20s, which the police describe as "extremely heavy" fireworks bombs. In total the explosives contained about 10 kilos of flash powder. The owner's home was also searched. A further explosive was found there. The Tigrisdreef is located in the middle of the neighbourhood, the police stress. "That created an enormous explosion hazard and a major risk for local residents." All explosives have been seized and safely removed, the police say. Investigation is ongoing. The municipality has closed the basement storage unit. Laughing gas: Nearly forty cylinders of laughing gas were found in a garage unit on the Muylenborchdreef, also in Overvecht. These have been seized and that unit has also been closed. No one has been arrested for that yet, RTV Utrecht reports. The municipality of Utrecht and police carry out checks in garage and basement units more often. "It regularly happens that these spaces are used for criminal activities, for example for storing fireworks, explosives, flammable substances or other tools for explosive raids," according to the police.

title: Two ships set on fire after possible drone attacks off the Romanian coast
lead: Two commercial cargo ships caught fire off the coast of Romania last evening and overnight after possible Russian drone attacks. The vessels are two tankers that were at anchor in the Black Sea. Search efforts are ongoing for seven crew members from one of the ships, while other crew members have been brought to safety. The Black Sea, which borders not only Romania but also Ukraine and Russia, has been unstable for some time. This week, two other ships in the sea were also attacked; so far, at least six ships have been attacked in October. At least twenty crew members have been killed or gone missing as a result. It is still unclear whether the two struck oil tankers were hit by Russian drones, and research into this is ongoing. It is known, however, that the attacks took place within Romania's territorial waters. Multiple drones also violated Romania's airspace on Wednesday, according to <entity id="pos:minister-van-defensie">minister van Defensie</entity> Miruta. Ukrainian grain "These drone attacks are a direct result of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine," says Romanian President Dan. "They not only endanger shipping in our region, but also the vital supply of agricultural products to other continents." The attacked ships were a few kilometres from the Romanian Sulina Canal, which connects the Black Sea with the Danube river. The canal forms a crucial route for the export of Ukrainian grain. Ukraine exports a large amount of grain through the waters of neighbouring Romania, because export through Ukrainian ports is extremely risky due to Russian bombardments. The increased unrest in the Black Sea could endanger the global food supply. Both Russia and Ukraine supply a large part of the world with grain. Much of the harvested crops in both countries remain in the granary due to the war. NATO countries The earlier attacks this week took place off the Bulgarian coast. Romania and Bulgaria are both members of the NATO military alliance. Under the NATO treaty, if one of the countries is attacked, this also means an attack on other members of the alliance, such as the Netherlands. "We have agreed that Romania and Bulgaria will work closely together to press for stronger measures against drones within the EU and NATO," says the Romanian President after a conversation with his counterpart Radev of neighbouring Bulgaria. Both countries have reported multiple airspace violations by Russian drones in recent years.

title: Albert Heijn: supply to stores fully resumed, no home delivery yet
lead: Four days after Albert Heijn was hit by a (attempted) hacking attack, stores are being supplied again as before. "Regular deliveries of both shelf-stable products and fresh products to our stores have fully resumed across the country," the supermarket chain says in a brief update on the situation. Product availability may still differ from store to store, Albert Heijn says. Over the course of the day, there should be fewer and fewer empty shelves to see. No delivery and no saving Yet the situation is far from normal. Albert Heijn still does not deliver online orders. The AH website is also not yet back online. The savings programmes and personal bonus offers are also not yet working. Now that supply is running again, the chain says it is focusing on "carefully and safely restoring the full range of services". What exactly happened is still unclear. Albert Heijn says it took its IT systems offline itself because of a 'cybersecurity incident'. Conversations between NOS and people from the security world revealed that it was a hacking attack. The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> urged Albert Heijn yesterday to file a report. At that point, at least, this had not yet happened.

title: Harry and Meghan work towards a British comeback in familiar Notthingham
lead: Prince Harry and his wife Meghan have appeared together in public for the first time since their return to the United Kingdom. The couple visited several charities in the city of Notthingham in front of a large public audience. On arrival, Harry and Meghan took plenty of time to chat with the public and shake hands. According to the BBC, the crowd erupted when she stepped out of the car. One woman called out: "We love you, Duchess Meghan, we love you!" It is the first official public appearance since the couple moved from the US to England. For Meghan, it is her first public appearance in the United Kingdom in four years. The last time was at the funeral of Queen Elizabeth II in 2022. The welcome was warm in Notthingham: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back from their roles as members of the British royal family in 2020 and left the United Kingdom. They wanted to divide their time between the United Kingdom and California, where Meghan was born. In August it became known that Harry and Meghan, with their two children, Prince Archie (7) and Princess Lilibet (5), are moving back to the UK. According to British media, several factors play a role, including the wish to spend more time in Europe, having their children educated in the United Kingdom, and being closer to Harry's family. Cookery workshop Choosing Notthingham for such an open return is not entirely coincidental. In 2017, Harry and Meghan made their first official appearance there as an engaged couple. British media report that during their visit they will call on three social organisations. At Himmah Hub they will take part in a cookery workshop. Afterwards they will visit the organisation's food bank, where they will speak with people living in poverty. They will also visit youth organisation Community Recording Studio and Epic Partners, an organisation that supports children and families. Harry has been involved with Community Recording Studio and Epic Partners for more than ten years. Meghan previously worked with Himmah on Together: Our Community Cookbook, which was published in 2018. After leaving the United Kingdom, Harry and Meghan remained involved with British charities through their own foundation. But their focus lay elsewhere. Harry and Meghan gave their wish for "a quieter life" as the reason for leaving, but they also signed lucrative contracts with Netflix and Spotify. Their relationship with the rest of the royal family deteriorated quickly. The couple stated that palace staff had been insensitive to Meghan's mental health. They also accused other members of the royal family of racism and of manipulating the media. Harry's open criticism of his family and the royal household led to a rift between the prince and his father, King Charles. For years, the king did not see his grandchildren. Oxford Tensions have eased somewhat in recent months, now that Harry has expressed the wish to reconcile with his father. He has also said that he wants his children to get the chance to get to know their 77-year-old grandfather. Charles is currently being treated for a form of cancer that was diagnosed in early 2024. Harry, Meghan and their children are reportedly living in a home in the Cotswolds, an area of hills, villages and farms west of the city of Oxford.

title: Japanese companies to invest billions in American chip factories
lead: Japanese companies will invest up to 21 billion dollars in building two chip factories in the United States. These will be owned by the American government and Japanese investors. The plan is part of a larger deal between Japan and the <entity id="org:regering">de regering</entity> of Trump. Japan is investing a total of 550 billion dollars in the US in the coming years, in return for President Trump's promise to lower import duties on Japanese goods. That last part already happened immediately after the agreement was made: the duty on Japanese cars, for example, went from 25 percent to 15 percent. The US has, however, made it a condition that Japan actually carries out the investments. Management of the chip factories will be in the hands of GlobalFoundries, a large manufacturer in the semiconductor market. A semiconductor is the material a microchip is made of. The company does not sell its own chips, but produces them for others. Construction of the first factory is due to start by the end of this year. Chip production is intended to get going in 2029. At the end of 2028 a decision will be made on whether a second factory will actually be built. Dependence on China: On paper it is not a bad idea for Japan to invest in the American factories. The US is the largest buyer for most Japanese goods, including in the semiconductor industry and for sales of chip machines. Lower import duties are therefore advantageous. In addition, Japan wants to decouple more from China, the country from which Japan currently imports cheap chips. But above all, Japan wants to keep ties with the United States warm. That is important, partly because Japan is heavily dependent on the US for its national security. NOS op 3 made a video about the tensions between China and Japan: Japan also hopes it can earn something from the investment. Ideally, manufacturers of chip machines in Japan can sell their machines to the chip factories. Production moved back home: The United States, for its part, wants to pull the chip industry back towards itself. In recent years it has already made an enormous catch-up effort, but by American standards it is not yet enough. The US fears that the global supply chain will end up in Chinese hands. Despite all the ambitions, it is an open question whether the first factory will be finished on time and whether it can start running quickly. In America, wages and factory costs are high. In a similar project by the Taiwanese company TSMC, the largest independent manufacturer of semiconductor chips, construction of a factory in Arizona was considerably delayed. The United States very much wants to move forward, but does not always have the manpower and knowledge in-house to set up and keep running such advanced factories. In recent years America outsourced this kind of work to countries such as South Korea, Taiwan, Japan and the Netherlands. Criticism: It remains to be seen whether the Japanese investments prove financially sustainable. That thought is also alive among Japanese citizens. They criticise the plans and already see their money disappearing to the US. Japanese people have difficulty with Trump's fickleness: they see that it is hard to make firm agreements with the American president. More than a quarter of Japanese see the US as the greatest threat to world peace. Japanese citizens also want to become less dependent on China, but a large part of the population fears that the dependence is now shifting from China to the US. Japanese would rather see the country invest in its own industry. How can Japan invest billions? Japan's budget in 2025 was roughly 770 billion dollars, which means the country could never finance the mega deal itself. That is why the Japanese government urges companies to invest. The government offers subsidies, support and guidance for a greater presence in the American market. The construction of the chip factories in the US is not the first project under the recent trade agreements between Japan and the United States. Earlier, Toyota promised to invest up to 10 billion dollars in its American production facilities. Japanese CEO Masayoshi Son of technology investment company Softbank made a huge commitment at the end of 2024: within four years the company wants to invest 100 billion dollars in the US. That should yield some 100,000 jobs, focused on artificial intelligence. The CEO is a billionaire and has in the past more often had coffee with President Trump.

title: Podcast De Dag: The rise of the Houthi's
lead: Saudi Arabia is under fire from the Houthi's. After attacks on the country's main airport in the capital Riyadh, the armed fighters are also hitting oil installations and another airport. Flights to Riyadh are still at a standstill. Want to listen? You can listen to this episode of De Dag via NPO Luister and all other podcast apps. Like it? Don't forget to subscribe. Correspondent Daisy Mohr explains in the podcast De Dag how the Houthi attacks have intensified recently. Many people will know the group from seizing container ships in the Red Sea. But since the war between the US and Iran, the Houthis' options have expanded. Who can stop them? Respond? Email dedag@nos.nl Presentation & editing: Marco Geijtenbeek Editors: Judith van de Hulsbeek and Judith Kutschenreuter

title: Animal ambulance receives unexpected 50,000 euros from inheritance: 'Never expected'
lead: The Stichting Dierennoodhulp <entity id="org:provincie-flevoland">Flevoland</entity> is delighted with a large inheritance. The foundation has received no less than 50,000 euros from a man who died last year. Chairwoman Irma Moes of the Stichting Dierennoodhulp Flevoland had not seen the amount coming. The foundation had organised a digital collection for donations because of Animal Day when Moes was called and told the surprising news by an executor. Initially Moes assumed a donation of 100 euros. "Then that woman said: it is a much larger amount." She therefore had to swallow when the amount of 50,000 euros was mentioned. "We never expected this", she tells Omroep Flevoland. Animal lover The money was bequeathed by Joop van der Vaart, founder and former owner of an ice cream parlour in <entity id="org:gemeente-lelystad">Lelystad</entity>. He died at the beginning of last year at the age of 71. Moes did not know him personally, but according to her he did have a connection with the foundation. "Joop regularly called the dispatch centre of the animal ambulance because, for example, there was something with a little bird that needed to be picked up." Moes thinks Van der Vaart saw that her foundation does good work and that is why he decided to leave money behind. Rising fuel prices The Stichting Dierennoodhulp Flevoland is responsible for the animal ambulance and shelter in various municipalities in the province. The foundation also runs an animal shelter in Lelystad. According to Moes, the large sum comes in very handy. For example, it helps enormously to absorb the rising fuel prices and allows the animal ambulance to remain supported over the long term. "We have jointly decided to spread the amount over five years." The money can also help more animals. Moes explains that animals from the wild, unlike stray animals, do not fall under the responsibility of a municipality. The foundation therefore pays most of the costs of helping these animals itself.

title: Fierce battle over the world's most influential climate report: 'Never experienced before'
lead: It is make-or-break for the world's most influential climate report. It must be published before a decisive international climate summit in 2028, but the debate over the timing of publication is turning into a fierce political battle. The authoritative UN climate panel IPCC, currently meeting in Ethiopia, is creaking and groaning as countries are at each other's throats. In the report, the seventh so-called assessment report of the IPCC, hundreds of climate scientists from all over the world bundle all insights into global warming. It is considered the basis of international climate policy. Moreover, these IPCC reports are among the few things in the polarised climate debate on which almost all countries broadly agree in substance. In the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa, the 195 member states are negotiating, among other things, about the time they take for this latest report. The Netherlands, together with European countries and small island states, for example, would like to see it appear in 2028 as planned. But countries with large fossil fuel interests, especially Saudi Arabia and India, are trying to prevent that at all costs. Because it is precisely at the 2028 climate summit that countries must assess how much progress has been made toward achieving the Paris climate goals. There it was agreed to limit global warming to 2 degrees, and preferably even 1.5 degrees. For that assessment, such a bundling of the latest insights is of great importance, because then everyone bases themselves on the same and latest knowledge. Always a lot of drama. It is always haggling and theatre, says climate expert Leo Meyer, who has been involved with the UN climate panel since 1995. Even now, "supposedly retired", he advises the Dutch IPCC delegation independently. "But I have never experienced anything as hard as what is being played out now in all my years." IPCC expert Kari De Pryck of the University of Lausanne says the same. "This is truly without precedent. There has always been a lot of drama at the IPCC, but not about this." For about three years countries have been debating with each other, and the struggle reaches boiling point this week. If agreement fails to materialise, she foresees problems for the 2028 summit. "They certainly need input from the IPCC." Thick reports To what extent countries deliberately delay this report to get in the way of the independent climate scientists is not always clear. There are also poorer countries that argue for delay because they do not have the people and resources to comment on the thick reports in time. That problem plays much less or not at all in richer countries. "Participation and inclusiveness have been an issue from the very beginning. There has been great inequality from the start", says De Pryck. Poor countries, where fewer scientists usually have to do the work with less money, have therefore often had less input and are now putting on the brakes because they do not want to rush their work. But Saudi Arabia, for example, which also sides with this camp, is known in the field for "obstruction, attempts to slow down the IPCC and an anti-scientific attitude", says De Pryck. "I can still imagine that there is something legitimate in it for countries like Kenya", Meyer adds. "But Saudi Arabia, India, Russia and by extension China clearly embrace it. They really have an interest in pulling the teeth out of the IPCC reports." Behind the scenes it is said that the Saudis and the Indians in particular use the discussion about participation and inclusiveness to defend their fossil fuel industry. Political pressure Still, both experts emphasise that the world is not groping in the dark without a timely report. "Of course it is not the case that countries would have absolutely no idea. Like: 'hey, is there a climate problem? Gosh, let's just wait for those IPCC reports'", Meyer jokes. "But in terms of political pressure, it of course has a lot of influence. That diminishes if you cannot quote from the latest IPCC report." Ideally, the countries hope to have settled the political struggle by tomorrow at the latest, so that the budgets can be determined and the independent scientists know when their work is expected. If that does not happen tomorrow and they have to continue into the weekend, the question is whether enough representatives will still be left in Ethiopia to be able to vote at all.

title: Netherlands and France talk for the first time about cooperation on nuclear weapons
lead: Delegations from the Netherlands and France have for the first time held talks about cooperation in the field of nuclear weapons. That is what the <entity id="org:ministerie-van-defensie">ministerie van Defensie</entity> reports. The discussion, yesterday in Paris, did not come out of nowhere: President Macron announced in March that he wanted to talk with several other European NATO countries, including the Netherlands. The Netherlands and France discussed ways to "strengthen European nuclear and conventional deterrence", the Ministry of Defence reports. The security relationship between the two countries in general was also discussed. According to defence minister Yesilgöz, an important step has been taken with the talks. "In this way we are taking responsibility for our own security", she wrote on social media. The talks between NATO countries could lead to French nuclear weapons being stationed in other European countries. That also happens with American nuclear weapons: those are located, for example, at the Dutch air base in Volkel. Dependence on the United States European NATO countries want to become less dependent on the United States in the field of defence. According to <entity id="person:tom-berendsen">minister Berendsen</entity> of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">Buitenlandse Zaken</entity>, "the American nuclear umbrella remains the foundation". He does state that Europe must take more responsibility for its own defence. Besides the Netherlands and France, the United Kingdom, Germany, Poland, Belgium, Greece, Sweden and Denmark take part in the French initiative. The only two countries in that cooperation who possess nuclear weapons are France and the UK. France is expanding its arsenal, the UK has a smaller number of warheads. French submarines France has four nuclear submarines. One of them is always on patrol. That is to ensure that a retaliatory nuclear strike can be launched at any moment if necessary. The French president is the only one who can order a nuclear strike, but is supposed to abide by the non-proliferation treaty, which states that the use of nuclear weapons is restricted. The four missile submarines have room for ballistic missiles and warheads. Each submarine carries sixteen ballistic missiles, each equipped with six to ten warheads. The nuclear weapons are many times more powerful than the atomic bomb the US dropped on Hiroshima in 1945 and can hit targets more than 6000 kilometres away.

title: Alcohol ban at German train stations takes effect after violent incidents
lead: Having a quick beer, downing a liqueur shot or knocking back a schnapps is no longer possible at German train stations. Today an alcohol ban has taken effect at all 5700 train stations in Germany. The alcohol stop was already announced last summer . The railway company Deutsche Bahn (DB) introduced the ban to improve safety at stations. According to DB, thousands of violent incidents took place in Germany last year. A serious accident involving a train conductor was the last straw for the company. Last summer the conductor fell out of a moving train after he was beaten up by an intoxicated passenger without a ticket. The conductor was seriously injured. Difficult to enforce The ban on consuming alcohol applies in all station buildings and on platforms. There are exceptions for restaurants, cafés and on the trains themselves. Although DB has introduced the ban, the company still sells alcohol on its own trains. Earlier, Germany's largest police union warned that the ban is likely impossible to enforce unless extra police officers are added. Offenders will initially only be informed of the ban, but whoever lets the situation escalate risks an area ban. Experimenting with an alcohol ban Ahead of the nationwide ban, DB experimented with a ban on alcohol consumption at a few stations in large cities. According to the railway company, fewer violent incidents took place as a result. DB stresses that the ban also applies on public holidays and during major events. Having a beer before a football match or on the way to Oktoberfest has thereby become at least more difficult.

title: Execution of major who carried out attack will not be broadcast live after all, says Trump
lead: The execution of former soldier Nidal Hasan will not be broadcast live. That is what the American president Trump writes on his platform Truth Social. "He will, as planned, be executed by firing squad, but this event will not be broadcast," said Trump. Nidal Hasan was a major and worked in the army as a psychiatrist when he shot thirteen people dead at a military base in 2009. He was sentenced to death, to be carried out by the army. Last Tuesday it became known that this would be done by firing squad. Last week Defense Minister Hegseth said he wanted to livestream Hasan's execution. It would thereby be the first public execution in the US in ninety years. 'Powerful deterrent' Initially President Trump approved the plan, but he is now backing away from it. "I think broadcasting the execution could have been a powerful deterrent for the world to see how America deals with terrorists and scum like Hasan," he writes. "However, many decent and well-meaning people would rather not see him die via a livestream or any other visual medium." According to Trump, the closest family members of the victims will have the opportunity to attend the execution in person, should they wish to. The execution is scheduled for 3 December, but due to appeal procedures it is questionable whether that date will be met. First time in sixty years It is the first time since 1961 that the American army carries out a death sentence. It also very rarely happens that a convicted person in the US is killed by firing squad. That has happened only six times since 1977, out of 1684 executions. Most death row inmates were given a lethal injection .

title: JA21 and SGP reject compulsion in housing asylum seekers
lead: JA21 and SGP want "in writing" a commitment from <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> that municipalities will not be forced to take in asylum seekers, which they must do under the dispersal act. That is what JA21 <entity id="person:bernard-johannes-eerdmans">leider Eerdmans</entity> said after his meeting with minister Van den Brink of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-am">Asiel en Migratie</entity>. Furthermore, they want tens of thousands of Syrians with a temporary residence status to be reassessed quickly, because parts of the country can be assessed as safe in their case and they may have to return. The cabinet must also quickly organise that asylum procedures take place outside the Netherlands and that in general the influx of asylum seekers goes down quickly. These demands come on top of the demand that the burdens on citizens in the Tax Plan must go down. For the two parties this is one of the conditions for supporting the Tax Plan and the budgets of the ministries before the end of the year. Lower burdens on citizens. The two parties together with the coalition parties have a majority in <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>. In <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Eerste Kamer</entity> they can also help the cabinet to a majority with other parties, but that is a lot more complicated. That majority is needed to approve the budgets. Without it the cabinet in principle may not spend money or levy taxes. Eerdmans does not yet want to say whether his party is already that far: "It is connected. We vote on the Tax Plan on 12 November. When we know the whole package, we will know whether we can vote for it." The talk with Van den Brink will be continued. What it means for the minority cabinet to go 'over left' or 'over right' has become somewhat clearer again. But how it will end is still uncertain. According to asylum minister Van den Brink these are not insurmountable demands in themselves. "I think I am able to keep working with JA21 on asylum and migration," he said after his visit to Eerdmans. Compulsion perhaps not needed. According to Van den Brink he is already working on most of the 'asylum demands' but is "only just started" as minister. About the dispersal act he says it simply has to be implemented. But he expects to "manage" with the municipalities. In other words: compulsion will in his view not be necessary. Asked whether his demands are not too high for the minority cabinet, Eerdmans answered: "The left asks six billion euros. We ask for asylum measures and those will rather bring in money. So I don't think at all that we are overasking." The left-wing opposition party Pro has demanded in negotiations with the cabinet that the cut on social security, such as the WIA and the WW, be taken off the table, in exchange for support for the budget of the ministry of Social Affairs. For the rest of the finances Pro has not yet guaranteed support.

title: Deceased wrong-way driver on A2 near Breukelen had become unwell
lead: The person who died last Saturday in a collision on the A2 near Breukelen had become unwell while driving. Research has shown this, according to the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>. The motorist was driving in the direction of Utrecht and at some point lost control of the steering wheel. The car shot through the central reservation and ended up on the road towards Amsterdam. There the car collided with two other cars. The wrong-way driver did not survive, and one of the two other drivers was injured. The police are not disclosing the age and home town of the deceased driver. No guardrail On the relevant stretch of the A2 between Breukelen and Vinkeveen there is no guardrail, writes RTV Utrecht. The carriageways are separated for several kilometres by a grass strip. Every few hundred metres there is a short piece of guardrail. In 2019 a similar accident happened on the same stretch of the A2. Three people died then: the wrong-way driver himself and a couple who were in another car. New research A spokesperson for <entity id="org:rijkswaterstaat">Rijkswaterstaat</entity> told RTV Utrecht yesterday that it is simply not possible to place a guardrail everywhere. Rijkswaterstaat manages a total of over 3000 kilometres of motorway. "Installing and maintaining a guardrail costs money. And if an accident happens, that also requires extra maintenance." Rijkswaterstaat's policy is that no guardrail needs to be placed on a verge wider than 20 metres. Following Saturday's accident, Rijkswaterstaat is again researching traffic safety at the location in question. Whether a guardrail will come is not yet clear for the time being. "Ultimately we always ask: how can we arrange it cost-effectively while at the same time ensuring everyone can drive safely."

title: Dutch knowledge platform Raam placed on blacklist in Russia
lead: The Dutch knowledge platform Raam, which shares information about Russia and Eastern Europe, has been designated an undesirable organisation in Russia.
